    "description": "This is the final episode of the Sarah Paine lecture series, and it’s probably my favorite one.\n\nSarah gives a “tour of the arguments” on what ultimately led to the Soviet Union’s collapse, diving into the role of the US, the Sino-Soviet border conflict, the oil bust, ethnic rebellions and even the Roman Catholic Church. As she points out, this is all particularly interesting as we find ourselves potentially at the beginning of another Cold War.\n\nAs we wrap up this lecture series, I want to take a moment to thank Sarah for doing this with me. It has been such a pleasure.\n\nIf you want more of her scholarship, I highly recommend checking out the books she’s written. You can find them here: https://www.amazon.com/stores/S.-C.-M.-Paine/author/B001HCVOTG\n\n𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/sarah-paine-cold-war\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/dwarkesh-podcast/id1516093381?i=1000742025593\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/5MF73tDb0Nw9Bt7O5oIsIV?si=04d739580dd14269\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n- Labelbox can get you the training data you need, no matter the domain. Their Alignerr network includes the STEM PhDs and coding experts you’d expect, but it also has experienced cinematographers and talented voice actors to help train frontier video and audio models. Learn more at https://labelbox.com/dwarkesh\n- Sardine doesn’t just assess customer risk for banking & retail. Their AI risk management platform is also extremely good at detecting fraudulent job applications, which I’ve found useful for my own hiring process. If you need help with hiring risk—or any other type of fraud prevention—go to https://sardine.ai/dwarkesh\n- Gemini's Nano Banana Pro helped us make many of the visuals in this episode. For example, we used it to turn dense tables into clear charts so that’d it be easier to quickly understand the trends that Sarah discusses. You can try Nano Banana Pro now in the Gemini app. Go to https://gemini.google.com\n\nTo sponsor a future episode, visit https://dwarkesh.com/advertise.\n\n𝐓𝐈𝐌𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐌𝐏𝐒\n00:00:00 – Did Reagan single-handedly win the Cold War?\n00:15:53 – Eastern Bloc uprisings & oil crisis\n00:30:37 – Gorbachev's mistakes\n00:37:33 – German unification and NATO expansion\n00:48:31 – The Gulf War and the Cold War endgame\n00:56:10 – How central planning survived so long\n01:14:46 – Sarah's life in the USSR in 1988",

      "id": "UgwPcijMjPFGF3_7Hkl4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "59:48 A massive computer network was proposed for the Soviet Union, with terminals in factories reporting back the actual figures to the Central Planning Committee - and they did have the technological capability to implement this. It was shot down by all the members of the Communist Party - because then all their lies about the production numbers, and all their little scams, grifting here and there and skimming off the top for their own enrichment - would become impossible! Everyone was lying about production numbers, just so that factory owners would get their bonuses for reaching their quota. Then those erroneous numbers were used by the Central Planning Committee - and it's a case of GIGO \"Garbage In, Garbage Out\". That's how you end up with massive shortages of things people actually want, like meat, clothing, TVs and cars - and you also get overproduction of stuff that people don't want, such as tins of seaweed and some tinned fish that tasted disgusting. Soviet people had to buy some of these unwanted goods before they would be allowed a coupon which permitted them to purchase things that they did want! There is a channel called Ushanka Show, which is run by a gentleman who grew up in the USSR, and he explains how all these systems \"worked\"!",

      "id": "UgwtAv2Ohvn2Ad2o7qx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Brilliant lecture by Sarah Paine, but it’s a narrative designed to soothe the American ego rather than explain the cold reality of history. If you look at it from the perspective of those who actually lived it, the story isn't one of Western \"victory,\" but of strategic betrayal:\n\n    The USSR wasn't defeated; it was surrendered: Paine credits Reagan’s pressure, but the Soviet Union was a self-sufficient fortress. It collapsed because Gorbachev was naive enough to believe in a \"Common European Home.\" He handed over the keys to the empire expecting partnership. Instead of a handshake, the West gave Russia the shock therapy of the 90s and pushed NATO to its doorstep despite every verbal assurance.\n\n    The Helsinki \"Trojan Horse\": We celebrate human rights, but from the Russian side, Helsinki was the first experiment in \"color revolutions.\" It wasn't about ethics; it was a weapon used to dismantle a sovereign state from within. What Paine calls \"liberation,\" the Russian people experienced as a 40% drop in GDP, a collapse in life expectancy, and the rise of oligarchs mentored by Western economists.\n\n    A Mirror for Modern America: Paine warns about the USSR’s internal rot, debt, and ideological blindness. The irony is palpable. While we lecture the world on the \"death of the Soviet system,\" the U.S. is currently repeating the same mistakes: massive over-leverage, crumbling domestic infrastructure, and an obsession with exporting a brand of \"democracy\" that creates more chaos than stability.\n\nThe Soviet Union died of imperial overstretch and a crisis of faith. By celebrating our \"victory\" instead of analyzing our failures in the post-1991 settlement, we have turned a potential partner into a permanent adversary. Triumphalism isn't history—it's propaganda.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The reason empires such as the Soviet Union die is from internal rot.  In the case of the Soviet Union the Russian people lost faith in the communist system. As usual there were more with needs than there were those with ability.  Those that were producing got tired of working without hope of advancement to supply all those with needs.   \nThe Afghan-Soviet War was just one more example that communism was not wanted by all people.  It also showed that the feared Soviet army could be defeated.  The Solidarity movement in Poland, and the election of a Polish pope showed that people did not want communism and its atheism.   Economic sanctions on a tottering system added to the decline of life quality in Russia until the people were fed up with it all by 1990.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "A dead tree can’t remain standing for a hundred years.\nRegan giving it a little push, despite intellectuals insisting at the time that ‘communism is inevitable’, is an achievement.",

    {
      "id": "Ugzmo7S9n5LcnSxbPed4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "One thing I found interesting about this, is Dr. Paine identifies the USSR's Satellite states not being effective allies and being a detriment to the soviet economy. Is their a reason she avoids diagnosing modern Europe in this same way in its relationship to the US? Because personally, that's the conclusion I have to draw when I look at the situation. It seems like Europe is getting a far better deal out of us than we're getting out of them. In hard currency we contribute about 16% NATO's operational costs, but when you factor in the deterrent that is our military it's something like 60-70% of all NATO nations military spending combined. When I see Trump waving his finger, I see the worlds dominant super power that is essential to everyone else' existence trying to get it's allies in line, not lose them. \n\nThat was touched on a bit with the 'institutions' focus. We've sort of hit a point where the good Dr. might argue we need a refresh across the entire western world. Right now you look at the Ukraine situation, and Europe is one of Russia's primary funders by way of oil purchases. Why are they doing this? Because their institutions demand they conform to a green policy that shuffles their 'dirty work' to other parts of the globe, so they can praise themselves about how much they are while having next to no effect on the problems they claim to care about. I see Trump amping up US production, and getting Venezuelan manufacturing up and running, and I 1) Russia running out of money to fund it's war without anymore escalation, and 2) Europe becoming MORE prosperous with greater access to cheap energy. I can't think of a reason that wouldn't have a similar effect as people under the Soviet union seeing the contrast with the west and getting a taste of something better. That sounds like a self correcting mechanism for institutions, or at least opens up the conditions where people who know what they're doing can then go in and make the appropriate corrections. \n\nI'd also be curious to know what Dr. Paine thinks about McKinley's tariff policies at the dawn on the industrial revolution, and their effect on developing the US economy. Because when I look at Trump's tariff policies, I see a lot of similarities in application, but to catch the wave of the coming AI and robotics revolution. It seems like a simple question to answer to me, would I rather China catches that boom or the US? Because it's coming regardless of whether or not you plan for it. \n\n\nI really enjoy Dr. Paine, she's fantastic. Can't wait to watch more! Thanks for hosting her.",

      "text": "\"You and I are told increasingly we have to choose between a left or right. Well I'd like to suggest there is no such thing as a left or right. There's only an up or down.       "id": "UgyvdfJ4JDQc9yR7uV14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "She is great, but she has some serious misconceptions about Russia and the EU, and she waves the word \"institutions\" around like some broad-stroke magic wand for every problem.\nShe doesn't seem to understand that many in the EU absolutely HATE the EU and its vaunted institutions, and why many Russians support Putin and the war in Ukraine.\nStarting with the Russian people, Putin has immensely improved Russia since the 1990s. Life in Moscow is now better than in Western Europe. Upper-middle-class Russians used to think about moving to Western Europe because it was better in every way; the ones that went are now very disappointed with life in the West, and they prefer life in Moscow. Russia after the USSR was an absolute Wild West. They hated Gorbachev because perestroika was a disaster. The Russians experienced so much upheaval and economic mismanagement. The improvement and stability Putin brought to the everyday lives of the Russian people is evident the second you actually talk to people there, rather than reason from an outside perspective. (She commits the exact mistake here that she herself warns about.)\nIt's a very similar story with the EU and the institutions she lauds so much: total disconnect from what the actual people are thinking. The EU is deeply unpopular. They did referendums in the beginning, but when they didn't like the results, they stopped. Their concerns are not addressed. These institutions are not here to do what the people want (democracy); these institutions now see the people as a problem to steer, not a people to listen to and serve.\nI'd love to hear a more in-depth conversation about institutions and why they are deeply unpopular with the people—a bit more in-depth, rather than just waving around the word \"institutions\" as if it's all great and solves everything. People want these institutions under new management, and that's exactly what will happen because every single great power wants this: the current US, Russia, China, and many, many people within the EU itself.",

      "id": "UgwbGa2Qrzvl05G8GJN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "One correction (17:15): the protests in the Eastern Block, or at least in Czechoslovakia (but I think it applied everywere else as well) were very much for political freedom as well. The people wanted not only freedom from Moscow but more importantly freedom from their terrible governments. The people wanted freedom, democracy and capitalism. \n\nThey wanted free and fair elections, freedom of speech, prosperity (meaning capitalism), environment protection, amnesty for political prisoners... freedom from Moscow was one of the things but that was much more considered automantic. Getting rid of the Czechoslovakian communist government included cutting ties with Moscow and joining the West, but getting rid of the Czechoslovakian communist government was the main goal. \n\nThe sign in the centre of the picture (17:07) says \"Down with the rule/government of batons\". And they meant the Czechoslovakian government, not the Soviet government.  Batons were used by police against the demonstrating people so it was also demand for freedom of gathering specifically  and end of the use of violence to repress the people generally.  \n\n'Havel to the Castle' was one of the most common slogans of the demonstrations - Václav Havel was the most known disident who was in prison at the time and the Castle meant the Prague Castle which was and still is the presidential residence, so the slogan meant 'free Havel (and others) from prison and make him the president'.  That was very much about political freedom. They wanted regime change.  Another extremely common slogan was 'End the one-party rule.\" They wanted democracy and did not want to settle with anything less.\n\nFun fact: the communists really freed Havel (and others) from prison and made him the president.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "As a French young man, I can say the US are almost at a point of no return concerning relations with the younger generation of at least its Western European allies (I can't really say for Eastern Europe, as they feel far more threatened by the likes of Russia). We know that now, US actions can drasticly change because of elections, which already makes the US an unreliable ally. The only reason I, personally, think that alliance with the US is still worth it is because the other options (Russia and China) are objectively worst than the actual situation apart from maybe a stronger European Union, if we can get rid of most European politicians, that are clearly not statesmen. Now, if Trump decides it is time to take Greenland by force, like he just did with Venezuela (I am actually happy that Maduro is no more at the head of Venezuela, I am more worried about what Trump wants to do with it), I would say that any alliance with any European Nation would be null and void.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Sarah is great, but she is right: she is just an academic that was given a podium. And I mean that in a good way. There are hundreds if not thousands of other professors that can talk just as well as her. They just need a podium. I am a history student in the Netherlands and have already met some of these people. If they were native English speakers, you could have them on here and do just as well. My ancient history teacher is one such man for example. He tells stories so vividly, but is also able to link Athenian struggles with democracy to those in the Netherlands (and many other countries in the west) today. Ye can break down complex examples into general principles that work for all societies. There are so many lessons to be understood, about the recent and distant past, that people would do well to hear. So if you can find another of these academic gems, we are here to listen to them.",

      "id": "UgwlEdpIQc1X6SYQmqZ4AaABAg",

      "id": "Ugx1sIBT8NeT17n2mct4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I grew up in Russia in the 1990s and I would disagree with a couple of minor points in this discussion (overall the lecture is superb). There were plenty of entrepreneurial and business minded young men and women in Russia that could have flourished economically post USSR. The problem was that the country had no idea on how to enforce private property ownership. So racketeering and organised crime sprung up overnight to come and terrorise whatever small business or company was being set up, from market stall to supermarket or restaurant. The organised crime cartels grew and eventually morphed into government, and this paved the way for the oligarcho-capitalist Russia of today which evolved from the criminalised post privatisation Russia of the 90s. About the help of western experts with economic reform - many of them did actually come in 1991, and years after that. Many consultants from American and British investment banks (big names like HSBC) roamed the halls of the ministry of commerce and such at that time advising Russia on how to do privatisation and market integration. Suffice it to say, the result of these \"reforms\" was a total failure. I don't know who asked them to come, but it's clear (at least now) that the country lacked basic institutions in place before it could or should have been hacked apart and sold on the \"free\" market to the highest bidder. Neither was anyone particularly interested in nuclear disarmament after 1991. It would have been much easier to force disarmament on Russia at that time with economic measures, than it will be in the coming years (fingers crossed to be wrong on this). So let's praise the Bush/Kohl administration on the Germany deal, but by God let's not forget that the collective west did mess things up an awful lot when it came to its Russia policy with Yeltsin in the 90s.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCJOargLq0u5QbjxAJeTk7Pg",

      "text": "⚪🔴⚪Беларусь знаходзіцца паміж НАТА ( які вырабляе каля 60% сусьветнага ВУП) і Маскоўскай імперыяй ( менш за 1%) . З аслабленьнем Маскоўскай імпэрыі праз вайну ва Ўкраіне Крамлю патрэбная бясьпечная мяжа, каб пазьбегнуць прамога сутыкненьня з Захадам. У гэтай сытуацыі нейтральная Беларусь павінна стаць ключавой нейтральнай дзяржавай ў Еўропе , якая гарантуе стабільнасьць і пакой усім суседзям. 3 Прыклады з гісторыі : У 1955 годзе Захад  і Бальшавіцкая імпэрыя падпісалі Аўстрыйскую Дамову, праз якую  Аўстрыі: «была нададзеная незалежнасьць і адбылося вывад усіх акупацыйных войскаў у абмен на абавязак Аўстрыі да вечнага нейтралітэту». І гэтая дамова дзейнічае нават сёньня, 40 гадоў пасьля краху бальшавіцкай імпэрыі. . Калі бальшавікі акупавалі Манголію, яны маглі яе анэксаваць і «маскоўфікаваць», як яны зрабілі з многімі іншымі дзяржавамі і народамі. Але замест гэтага яны пакінулі Манголію як буфэрную дзяржаву з Кітаем, разумеючы, што гэта для іх найлепшае рашэньне. Гэта зрабіла мяжу з Кітаем удвая карацейшай, і нават сёньня Маскоўская імпэрыя мае добрыя дачыненьні з Манголіяй. Іншы прыклад, Ўругвай,быў створаны ў XIX стагодзьдзі як буфэрная дзяржава паміж Аргентынай і Бразыліяй, у ХХ стагодзьдзі замацаваў сваю ролю нейтральнага пасярэдніка, што дазволіла яму пазьбегнуць рэгіянальных войнаў і ўмацаваць дэмакратыю ды сацыяльную сыстэму. Усе гэтыя прыклады паказваюць, што нейтралітэт РБ — гэта не слабасць, а адзіная лагічная Стратэгія ў нашай геаграфічнай рэчаіснасці . Беларусь можа зрабіцца Аўстрыяй - Ўругваем Усходняй Эўропы. І у практычнай лёгіцы Трампа, які вядомы сваімі міравымі дамовамі і кампрамісамі, гэта адзіны шлях, дзе ўсе бакі перамагаюць, Захад і Маскоўская імпэрыя  атрымліваюць:  стабільную — бясьпечную, ПАКОЙНУЮ мяжу, а мы беларусы — нацыянальную дзяржаву , свабоду, дэмакратыю, і дабрабыт.",

      "text": "There is something missed at min 20 that is very important:\n.\n.\n.\nDr Paine talks about the 'democratic' turn within the Communist block countries and yet no tanks from Russia rolled in to quash these uprising unlike Hungary of 1956.  There is a fundamental difference that was not mentioned:\n.\nThe Russians (Soviets) were out of cash - there was an attempt by the Soviets to give sovereign guarantees to a group of banks in exchange for money (I remember this well) but the entire deal fell apart. The situation was so dire that the Soviet Union who was once the biggest producer and exporter of wheat had become the biggest importer of wheat.\n.\nGorbachev turned to basically beg the Americans for assistance. In a particular meeting with the then president Bush (senior) - at the very end of the meeting, Gorbechev asked Bush if he could send military into East Germany to quell the uprisings. Bush at first said, \"what you do within the communist block is your internal affair\".... but as Bush left the meeting, he turned and told Gorbi, \"If you do that, the entire deal is off\".\n.\nIn essence, the Russians held off repeating the Hungarian experience, not because they had become nicer communists, but rather because they were desperate to keep a bigger whole together and they needed the American assistance.       "text": "The video mentions uprisings in Kazakhstan and Yakutia, but the largest mobilizations — both in absolute numbers and per capita — occurred in the Baltic states and in Georgia. Georgia likewise saw massive mobilization, with over 1.7 million total participants recorded across various demonstrations between 1987 and 1989. More broadly, data from 1987–1989 shows that over 80% of all recorded incidents of unrest in the USSR were concentrated in the Baltic republics and the Caucasus, including Georgia. Crucially, none of these republics ever fully accepted Soviet rule: expressions of loyalty by local party and administrative elites were largely formal and performative, while the population consistently viewed the regime as an occupation. In Georgia, resistance long predated Gorbachev — from the March 1956 Tbilisi protests (suppressed with lethal force), to the April 1978 mass demonstrations that successfully defended Georgian as the official state language, to the April 9, 1989 peaceful independence rally, violently dispersed by Soviet troops, killing 21 demonstrators and radicalizing society. Soviet control itself was uneven: due to Georgia’s mountainous terrain, regions such as Svaneti and Tusheti were only weakly penetrated by Soviet authority until the late 1920s–1930s, with resistance and limited state presence persisting long after the 1921 invasion.     {
      "id": "UgypT4zsR_trE5scpeV4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "She comes across as an expert and a dedicated historian, but in reality, her lectures are very ostentatious and rather superficial. What was she saying—one thing the USSR managed to create was a functional metro system? But what about space exploration? All those satellites, spaceships, space stations, the first man in space, Gagarin, and regular flights—all of it continues. But what about taking a country with 90% rural population and transforming it in 70 years into a society with 75% urban population? Nuclear power is another good example (even after the Chernobyl disaster, which occurred when everything began to collapse). At first, it was a cruel and inhumane political system, but after the Stalin era, under Khrushchev, Brezhnev, and Gorbachev, the USSR as a whole and its economy became increasingly bourgeois. There was a huge disproportion between military industries and the civilian economy, as well as genuinely poor management and governance—but that doesn't mean nothing was done economically. It seems Paine visited the USSR once during a severe crisis, and that's it—she's a lifelong expert, but much of what she says is simply inaccurate, and she lacks knowledge on a wide range of topics.",
      "like_count": 5,
      "author_id": "UCKcSzIdILcCrJJ1TgTFu9Ww",
      "author": "@Vendon-j6y",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kB-e-3d1p4ytuTR5x3YUZFIAHkxxFZy_2KHFYn2rte76VkJIG-rjHEojN9o8dDu9ogOA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgypT4zsR_trE5scpeV4AaABAg",
      "text": "Well my point is I haven´t heard anything, even of such superficial analysis you provided, from her, she just shares generalized blatant conclusions, citations and memories from one trip to USSR. I am far from defending the USSR economic model, obviously, it collapsed in the end, but you can´t deny its achievements and oversimplify it.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCKcSzIdILcCrJJ1TgTFu9Ww",
      "author": "@Vendon-j6y",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kB-e-3d1p4ytuTR5x3YUZFIAHkxxFZy_2KHFYn2rte76VkJIG-rjHEojN9o8dDu9ogOA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgypT4zsR_trE5scpeV4AaABAg.ARRRLZj687bAS6Lo71ycgx",
      "parent": "UgypT4zsR_trE5scpeV4AaABAg",
      "text": "Even North Korea has a metro system, and nuclear power, and a space program. What is your point?\nSoviet ‘achievements’ in agriculture are not something to celebrate.\nIndustrialisation was happening under the Czars, and in the earlier days Soviets modelled their industrialisation on USA and Detroit.\nRussia being the last European nation to industrialise is not an achievement. And 75% urban population is still backwards compared to Europe.\nThe Soviets were geologically blessed; ample farm land, ample natural resources. They were also reasonably well educated. But the only thing of value they exported was oil. They had to import food. Every piece of equipment they made locally was poor quality and backwards compared to USA and Europe.\nA successful USSR would have exported desirable consumer goods; food, clothing, electronics, appliances. It would have exported the heavy machinery needed to efficiently make these consumer goods, and it would have exported the energy and materials needed to run these machines. But this is impossible under communism.\nIf Russia was inhabited by Canadians, they would be the most successful nation of all time.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCA9KikiMzsQ-d4KwPKL-XIQ",
      "author": "@s4098429",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kCqIxLp7cWIN3cTtgkAD496E26g5gmy-oVXFQ0Sd0=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,

    {
      "id": "UgypT4zsR_trE5scpeV4AaABAg.ARRRLZj687bAR_XL-I2soz",
      "parent": "UgypT4zsR_trE5scpeV4AaABAg",
      "text": "What's impressive about the USSR was their mass industrialization in the interwar period and during WW2. Able to crush the mighty Wehrmacht. Their problem is that they ran a perpetual war economy after WW2 trying to arms race with the USA. Soviets never surpassed 40% of US GDP, yet they were shipping arms all over the world. China survived because they abandoned communist dogma, \"doesn't matter if the cat is black or white, what matters is if it can catch mice\". They were selfish and smart, they didn't bother exporting ideology they used their resources for themselves.\nAmerica needs to learn a thing or two from the USSR and China. Shipping billions of arms all over the world is not sustainable, and China isn't playing that game anyways. And instead of sticking to free trade dogma, we need to learn from Japan Korea China and how they hollowed out our industrial base through industrial policy and protectionism.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCNCpICTWxmJPg69_5zRimTw",
      "author": "@hjc7429",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kGJzQne4tLxXgvjd2qdB4-ZxFvdKrEml04CMC_OW9Qbpq0uVjTTkyvuZ_aG_JA0VwRMg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgypT4zsR_trE5scpeV4AaABAg",
      "text": "Regarding the urbanization my point is, let´s say France, in 1920s already 36% of its population was urbanized, in Spain 38%, in Italy 44%, in the Russian Empire transforming to the USSR - only about 15%.\nHowever, in 1991 (according to the Worldbank urban population data) urbanization in France - 78.8%, Spain - 75.03%, Italy - 66.7. In Russia in 1991 - 73.71%. What are you talking about?\nComparing North Korean \"achievements\" with those of the USSR is just ... that North Korean space program - \"roll-eyes\". They received their technologies from the USSR mostly in that epoch.",

      "text": "All that if \"Canadians were populating Russia\" rhetoric apart from xenophobic is, as well, questionable. \nFirst of all what part of Russia?       "id": "UgxcurD4dbrVMC9Gufh4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "There's a famous story that I think Gorbachev himself (edit, looked it up, it was Yeltsin in 89) related about the exact instant he released the USSR was doomed and the US would win. He took a trip to Texas and on the way from the airport to I think a ranch Reagan invited him to (pretty sure theres a pic of this visit in the video) he asked the delegation to stop at a regular, random grocery store in a podunk little town. It had thousands of varieties of food and served a tiny town in the middle of nowhere. Food that was considered a luxury and rare in the USSR was cheap and readily available in multiple choices to regular people. He was both struck with wonder and shocked. This was at a time where even stores that only catered to the high level party aparatchiks were facing shortages of goods. I think the grocery store was called Clarks (edit, it was called Randall's) but at any rate it broke down any notions that what they were seeing was fake propoganda and solidified in his mind they were on track to lose.\n\nI'm positive about the former story but theres an anecdote I heard about a NK General visiting Seoul. I wish I could remember enough to find the source or look it up but, I can't. Anyway the way the story goes, they're on the way to a conference and the NK general asks the SKs to take a right off the main road and then a left and a few other random turns. The South Koreans were confused and thought he was concerned about an an attack or something so they asked him why he requested the route change. His answer was to laugh and say \"You try too hard, we only bother with the front of the buildings.\" Meaning his thinking was so brittle it was litteraly inconceivable to him that what he was seeing was real and not some elaborate Potemkin Village. Gorbachev (edit: Yeltsin) was obviously more mentally flexible. Even today in NK, the \"nice\" grocery stores have fixed up facades and fake produce stacked up in front of windows but very little actual variety, or even food in general unless you're in the top 1% elite and visit special stores. Props to him for realizing they were on the wrong path, leading to reforms and ultimately Yeltsin dissolving the USSR relatively peacefully when the people rebelled and not going out in a spasm of violence and taking them with us in a nuclear exhange.",

      "text": "21:45 \"Das tritt nach meiner Kenntnis... ist das sofort... unverzüglich\"\n\nLegendary sentence of post-WW2 German history. \n\nWhenever you think you have screwed up, remember the guy who managed to screw up a simple press conference so bad it destroyed his state. \n\n(The actual idea of the travel regulations was that the borders guard were supposed to deface the travelling pass of whoever leaves, without their knowledge, so they don't come back.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "I think Sarah might have misread France's position and actions toward German reunification. Mitterand and Kohl had a great working relationship (they built the EU together, dragging Thatcher kicking and screaming into it). \nNot that it's always truthful, but I would advise to read Attali's memoirs from the Elysée (he was Mitterand diplomatic sherpa) wish shed some light on it.",

    {
      "id": "Ugwl97x-g2WdjzCOEfV4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "When you note that the 2025 Nobel Prizes for Economics are for showing the critical importance of \"innovation\" and \"creative destruction\" for economic growth, you also note that the old thinking about economic growth, capital, and labor may be wrong.  Then you note that government institutions are all effective monopolies in their areas, with no competition or failure mechanisms. You can note that the USA, before the recent evolution of the regulatory state, did allow even IBM to effectively kill its own bureaucracy as Apple, Microsoft, etc,  outcompeted IBM.\n\nThis evolution of monopoly institutions into frozen, incompetent organizations seems to explain why socialism/communism can have the best-sounding philosophy and belief system while consistently resulting in zero economic growth and little real innovation.   The USSR had its own IBM equivalent that copied IBM and probably borrowed a bit of IP, like the identical B-29 copy they made.    However, innovation put vacuum tube computers out of the market, and IBM had to adapt or die. By 1980, laptop computers became possible, while the IBM bureaucracy became as slow as any government monopoly, taking 7 years to design a new machine.  IBM owned the universe of my youth, but couldn't adapt to a bunch of bright kids in their parents' garages.   Note: AT&T Bell Labs invented the transistor, but the government monopoly phone systems were the last electronic system to switch to transistors from mechanical systems. \n\nTime and innovation played a huge factor in killing the planned economy of the USSR, and the economy killed the political government.   With China now producing massive numbers of high-quality STEM graduates and allowing them freedom to create and innovate in economic areas, our new \"industrial planning\" regulatory state, where it takes years to decades to get permission to implement any innovation, may fall to the state that allows innovation outside the USA.   China is poised to win, but its internal history of allowing innovation is marginal.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I will never forget a TV report from the USSR I saw as a child. A queue stretched at least a full city block, and a curious reporter asked, “What will you buy today?”\nA woman standing in line answered, “Whatever the shop has today.” \nIt was shocking to watch as a child — people didn’t even know whether there would be anything to buy.\nThose were the “good old days” of the USSR. It seems they may be returning sooner than expected.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Just started the lecture but if I may share some thoughts.\n\nThere is no single reason as to why the Soviet Union lost the Cold War, but if I may narrow it down. Its incompetence.\n\nWhat every authoritarian regime shares in common is incompetence. Their top down pyramid structures do not allow for competition and apposing views. Instead all information is brought to the top and trickled down by decree. This information choke hold does not stop there, as any information that is disadvantageous to the regime, the party, and its leader either shoots the messenger literally, puts them in prison, ostracizes them, or prevents their message from being heard. The rest is selectively gathered and shared so as to curry favor and or prevent becoming victim of the latter. \n\nThis lack information ranges on any issue and any conflict. From central planning to intelligence.\n\nEven IF coherent and honest information is shared with the ruler….that does not mean it will be listened to and acted upon. We have seen countless examples of authoritarians ignoring sage advice and  making decisions on emotion, ego, paranoia, fear, grandiosity and ideology.\n\nPropaganda can only go so far in ignoring reality, without it, the buffoonery would become immediately obvious.",

      "text": "Meh. She diminishes Reagan--literally raising him just to refute his contributions. Reagan grappled with the Cold War for 30 years before he even became president.       "text": "In a candid moment, Stalin once compared imposing Communism on Poland to \"fitting a saddle onto a cow\"—acknowledging the difficulty, if not the futility, of the task. \n\nHe wasn't wrong. That time, at least.",

      "text": "@Cdecisneros \n\nYou've got it backwards. Ford said in the '76 debate that Poland wasn't under Soviet domination—effectively claiming it was free and content with socialism.\n\n By contrast, Stalin's \"saddle on a cow\" metaphor admitted the reality, however grudgingly: communism had to be forced onto Poland with all available force because Poland was fundamentally incompatible with and deeply averse to Soviet rule and socialism as a governing system.",

      "text": "Paine is a strident anti-communist. And anti-communism is the twisted mutant lovechild of a long-standing traditional and violent rivalry between the British Empire and the pre-Soviet Russian Empire, in orgasmic conjunction with oligarchic capitalism's fixation on hating labor unions. So her basic point of view is corrupt, elitist, militarist and exploitationist. She twists the interpretation of facts egregiously. Her example of a revered historical scholar, Arnold Toynbee, was a figure who promoted the appeasement of Hitler in 1936 (after Hitler arranged to have Toynbee's ego suitably stroked) and antisemitic hatred of Jews throughout his sad career. \n\nEven discussing naval strategy, supposed the heart of her expertise, she is apparently unaware that nuclear-powered second-strike retaliatory submarines have nothing whatsoever to do with the rest of a nation's \"naval fleet,\" existing entirely separately and independently of the larger and far more costly war-fighting and power-projecting \"fleet.\" In fact no country with a second-strike submarine would ever deploy it for use in conventional war fighting such as sinking enemy ships. That isn't what second strike subs were built for or exist for. \n\nPaine's analysis of the CSCE conferences is equally \"painfully\" shallow. By 1970 all conceivable threats to the Soviet Union from the direction of Europe had completely collapsed, with Germany struggling to rebuilt after the devastation of WWII and France and England slowly sagging into insignificance under the weight of the costs of WWII piled on top of the costs of WWI. The new threat environment to the USSR came  primarily from the US, with a small supplemental nod in the direction of China. The USSR's accedence to the Helsinki Accords was viewed internally as a declaration of post-war triumph for the USSR, and a well deserved one at that, at least with respect to the USSR's external relations. Although internally the USSR was rapidly hollowing out under the crushing weight of its systemic criminal and social corruption along with the seductive pressure of western living standards fluttering just out of reach in front of the suffering Russian people. \n\nIf you want to reinforce your Goldwater, Nixonian and Reaganite prejudices then by all means watch this video.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "Wonderful interview, from an incredible series of interview.\n\nOne thing I have to say, though, from looking back at how the Soviet Union was run and fell, and the Cold War in general, there's one very important lesson I've taken from it. An entirely free market wouldn't work either, and we have plenty of historical proof of it doing far more harm than good before governments stepped in and ended overly capitalistic systems via regulations and limiting the free market.\n\nWithout a force to limit the extremes of any one system, perverse incentives tends to rule any system and thus cause downfall in the long run. But in some subjects I could have an opinion. \n\nThe most of the statements sounds good to me, but some are really ridiculous. Like no education. Yep, it's totally right that study of modern economics is a missing part, but it was in state's idiology to avoid all those buy / sale relations. But black market always existed. Otherwise, STEM discipline was one of the strongest in the world. And still is. I could compare for example IB MYP books with soviet math books. MYP is weaker. And current modern education in current public schools here in Baltics is just a total mess..\n\nAnd if you think that in 90ties anyone thought there in terms of \"democracy\" - think again. It was the survival mode for 10 years at least. Especially in the first 5 years.",

      "text": "Hi y’all, Abel here from San Francisco. I could relate so much to the VCR story—being from Cuba and a child of the Cold War myself (b. 1973).       "parent": "root",
      "text": "Around 2:00 ish:  I’m not sure if everyone understands Ronald Reagan’s change of mind, around 1986-87. My uncle was a colonel in the Airforce, stationed at Los Alamos and San Diego. He ended up seated close to Reagan - close enough to hear him, on several occasions, suggest that it would be just great to “nuke all the Ruskies”, and live underground for a few years. It was NOT presented as humor, at all. RR was serious.\nAnd once he took the White House, he also said similar things.       "id": "UgwsxjCrUWhEqMh5HKt4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Why, after the fall of the iron curtain, did Eastern Europe developed much faster and steadier than Russia?\nThree reasons: NATO, EU and the rule of law. Those are the very same reasons Ukraine wants to join the West.\n\nNATO and EU memberships created the conditions that allowed for a steady inflow of foreign investments. Also, the capital outflow (endemic in Russia) was reduced, and investments gradually improved the local economies.\n\nSarah Paine touched a key point with regards to the rule of law. Western European laws have at their core the Roman Law, especially private property laws. The Romans, especially in the Republican age, were first and foremost farmers. The long cycles between planting and harvest (think about olive trees) required stability and certainty of private property rights. Without it, farming is impossible.\n\nRussian laws and customs are instead based on Mongols' laws and customs. \nMongols were a nomadic people with almost no notion of private property. Under the Mongols, all the land belonged to the Khan, and it was the Khan who allocated plots of land to individual tribes for grazing.\r\nThe Mongols invented the Kolkhoz centuries before communism. And Russia is still stuck there. This is the root cause of Russia's misery.",

    {
      "id": "UgxTr7zrSV0FIjtm10F4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The point about the various contributions of US administrations leading up to the fall of the Soviet Union is very interesting and seems to have a lot of truth.\n\nOur system where the pendulum of political opinion seems to swing wildly every 2, 4, 8 years is jarring internally and feels inefficient but it also serves to keep our opponents off balance.  In this sense one might consider this a real advantage in that the US can triangulate onto the right course over time (even if we tend to overdo the reaction to unpopular policy initially).\n\nAlso, the rhetoric of Carter and Reagan seemingly couldn’t be any more different but the underlying power of the government (the bureaucracy and the military - the tribal knowledge) is not so changeable and tends to create stability between administrations.  The ideas and views of a president are what gets attention but, behind the scenes, these are tempered and moderated by the system the president is attempting to control\n\nThese effects can be seen today as well if you look for them.  I think it is something the most pessimistic political observers should keep in mind - a seemingly crazy and bad president will lead to something else and, amongst bad actions and mistakes, can very well contribute something unique and valuable that will (maybe unintentionally) prove useful to the next president",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCthDc9_l6mSutPDl60KeIug",
      "author": "@andrewlm5677",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_moMrxSyJ7Lp7CIJjGjpHrKPdt4XEe-YtGZ5e3U_UM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgxaNZuZH7yOrASEgTd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I can give a little insight of why the Soviets were still spending so much on Nuclear Weapons. In missiles in general, only so many get through. The \"enough nukes to destroy the earth multiple times over\" number doesn't account for missiles that are intercepted, because those missiles would still spread fallout and contribute to destruction long term. However, Nuclear deterrence is about second strike capacity. You not only need enough nukes to wreck your opponent, you need enough to survive their first strike, and to wreck them through their defenses. The Soviets were paranoid about the West, and they were going to continuously build up their stockpile under the assumption that the US first strike and defenses were getting better all the time.",

      "author_id": "UC3i2OOT4-c0vndivDRyyg6Q",

      "id": "UgxBZMwcbLU3Gt_uuqp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "As a citizen of the Czech Republic, some moments are almost comical. For example, the astonishment of Soviet politicians that Eastern Europe behaved so… ungratefully.\n\nWell then… the Czech Republic (or rather Czechoslovakia). We were living quite well, we started building socialism with a human face… and suddenly we hear a knock on the door.\n“Who’s there?” we ask.\n“It’s me, the Soviet Army. We heard you have a problem with capitalism, so I came to help you with that.”\n“That must be a mistake,” we reply.\n“That’s exactly what a capitalist would say! Comrades, we’ve found him—beat that capitalist to death before he infects anyone!”\n“What?” I barely manage to say. The front door flies open, the back door too, a few windows shatter. And tanks and soldiers start flooding into my apartment. Tens of thousands of soldiers. Some even start rappelling down the chimney.\n(Prague — 1968)\n\nOr should I mention the little “prank” they played on Poland? How they made a deal with Hitler… attacked. Then they rounded up all the captured teachers, doctors, priests, officers—basically everyone—and took them for a walk in the forest. And then they said: “You see that huge pit over there?”\nWith a satisfied sigh: “Well, it’s going to be full today.”\n\nAt that time, the Nazis had the opportunity to learn genocide from the already highly experienced USSR. In the Katyn Forest, up to 25,000 Polish prisoners from Poland’s elite were murdered.\n\nPoland never liked the USSR—there just wasn’t an opportunity for that sentiment to fully manifest.\n\nAs for Ukraine… genocide… Hungary… the massacre during the revolution…\n\nYou know, it’s hard to find anyone in Eastern Europe who didn’t want to see the USSR in ruins.\n\nSo after gaining freedom, our first question to the Soviets was:\n“Your army… um… when is it leaving? We’ve already prepared the trains.”",

      "text": " @landontesar3070  After the Second World War, 10-million-strong Belarus ⚪🔴⚪ lost around 3 million of its people. However, nearly 2 million had already been killed before the war by the Bolshevik colonial empire. In Belarus, 80 percent of all Belarusian writers were physically exterminated, along with scientists and artists. (The troupe of the Third Belarusian State Theatre of Uladzislau Halubok was arrested in full. Almost all were executed.) People were killed based on their national identity. For this, the label “natsdem” was invented (meaning “national democrat,” although no such party existed). This label was stuck onto all Belarusians whom the Stalinists planned to eliminate.\nDeep within the NKVD, a fictitious anti-communist organization called SVB (“Union for the Liberation of Belarus”) was fabricated. Under this phantom, NKVD agents carried out arrests, conducted imaginary investigations, interrogated, tortured, sentenced, then exiled people to the Moscow Empire and executed innocent individuals.\nAfter the Riga betrayal of 1921, Belarus was divided between Poland and the Moscow Empire. The border was drawn near Minsk. A secret NKVD directive ordered the extermination of all Belarusian population along the border. The Moscow occupiers wanted to create a depopulated zone. The extermination was carried out by border troops. Trusted agents were given a rifle and a shovel. If such a border soldier encountered a lone Belarusian man, woman, or child in a deserted place (on the road, in a field, in the forest), he would shoot the person, dig a grave with the shovel, and bury the body on the spot. That was the instruction. People in villages feared not “the man with the gun” as much as “the soldier with the shovel.” (These facts were published in the Belarusian press in the early 1990s.)\nIn the 1930s, 95–99 percent (virtually all) of the Belarusian communist-party and Soviet administration was exterminated (exiled and executed). Even directors and economic managers were eliminated. The positions of the murdered Belarusian administrators and communist officials were filled by “Muscovites” from the Moscow Empire. These “Muscovites” 🇷🇺 (so-called “appointees”) arrived in Belarus, took over the vacant posts, received privileges, property, apartments—and the first thing they did was shut down Belarusian schools and switch them to the “Moscow” language so their children could study without the burden of learning what they called the “useless” Belarusian language. In this way, the occupiers created a “Moscow-speaking” population in Belarus. Ethnocide, linguacide, mnemonicide, and genocide were carried out by the Bolsheviks simultaneously.\nThe extermination of Belarusians by the Moscow NKVD continued even during the German occupation. In June 1941, in the first days of the war, communists executed thousands of prisoners in jails and during transfers. Only in the Brest Fortress, which housed a terrifying NKVD prison, they didn’t manage to liquidate all detainees—some escaped. Meanwhile, a large group of NKVD guards and officials were trapped in the fortress by the Germans. They remained there for about a month until they died off. Twenty years after the war, communists invented the legend of the “heroic defense” of the Brest Fortress.\nIt is notable that the broad Soviet partisan movement was organized only in Belarus and partially in ethnically Belarusian lands that were part of the Moscow Empire (Smolensk region, Bryansk region). In the occupied Moscow Empire, there was no partisan movement. Why? Because the plan to exterminate the Belarusian nation continued. Moscow, using NKVD organs, dragged masses of civilian Belarusians into the war against the Germans, thereby exposing Belarusians to German retaliation. A necessary struggle was born of a treacherous scheme and carried out by vile methods. (Stalin wanted to reap double benefit.) NKVD agents would deliberately kill a German near a Belarusian village or stage another provocation to trigger a punitive operation by the Nazis (who typically burned the entire village, often with its inhabitants). Thus, as a result of a Bolshevik partisan provocation, the famous village of Khatyn was burned—later, in the 1970s, communists promoted it worldwide as a typical victim of fascist atrocities.\nAs a result of this joint Bolshevik–fascist “work,” more than 9,000 villages were burned in Belarus. By the end of the war, due to a special NKVD operation, many Belarusian commanders were sent to their deaths, removed from command, killed, and repressed. Their places were taken by Muscovites sent from Moscow and loyal NKVD agents.\nIn the summer of 1944, when the Red Army occupied Belarus, the Muscovites conducted a military mobilization on Belarusian territory. Tens of thousands of young Belarusian men, almost without training, were thrown onto the front lines. Moscow commanders sent them into pointless attacks under German machine-gun fire, often without even giving them weapons—or with rifles but no ammunition. They died by the thousands, like grass under a scythe. Those who fled were shot by NKVD “blocking detachments.” In fact, the blocking detachments shot people in the back. Thus, the extermination of Belarusians continued during the war—by the hands of both Germans and Muscovites. As the communists said, “in the struggle for the Soviet motherland.”\nIn the 1940s, Muscovites deported to Siberia and tortured all foresters and so-called “kulaks” from Western Belarus. They were deported in train cars, according to quotas.",

      "text": "My favorite Cold War German story is about coffee.  Germans love their coffee, be they from East or West.  The ultimate gift you could give an East German is Western coffee \nThe East Germans have to spend huge amounts of forgien capital to buy it.  East German coffee was notoriously bad.  As I said there was no better gift to give East Germans was decent coffee.\nThe DDR decided to come up with a cunning plan to solve their coffee problem.  They would invest their money in another Communist nation that could grow their coffee for them Vietnam. \nThe ironic part comes in because it takes time to grow a coffee tree before it starts producing beans.  By the time the trees were mature enough to harvest good beans, East Germany no longer existed.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "it's a shame the video only highlights the negatives, painting all Russians as bad or wrong. This ignores the tragic history where Russians suffered the most under communism—famines, purges, and millions of deaths.\nRussians aren't a single group defined by stereotypes from the Cold War era. Before the 1917 Revolution, many built huge wealth through hard work and innovation, like industrialist Nikolai Vtorov, who rose from humble beginnings to become one of Russia's richest men with factories, banks, and mines.Or the Morozov family, who created a textile empire employing thousands.\nAfter the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991, Russians showed resilience by rebuilding from scratch. Oligarchs like Roman Abramovich started small (selling toys from his apartment) and grew into billionaires through oil deals and investments. Vladimir Potanin built his fortune in metals with Norilsk Nickel, while Mikhail Khodorkovsky did the same in oil with Yukos. These stories highlight entrepreneurship in tough times.\nBoxing an entire nation as lazy and mean like this is extremely prejudiced and not helpful.",

      "text": "As much as i hate to say it, her views seem very one sided american to me. And that too americanized views after world war 2.       "text": "​ @varana Agreed with first one, i wanted to show that allies always keep on changing and they almost never remain the same during 2 consecutive conflicts, so i feel like that statement is a bit ambiguous.\n\n2nd one logic - China was getting bashed by japan, britsh and even russians for a 100 years.       "text": "Small correction. West Germany officially recognized Polish West Border (with East Germany) in 1970. It was a very important step toward a better future. What happened in 1990 was unified Germany repeated it officially and both nations mutually asked for forgiveness and friendship.",

      "author": "@januszchojnowski4009",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_noKH07iDe-Mebh3S1zSCmbRxinUe2ECDLn4I3v5Dk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgwV110DAtiHLSjmBBl4AaABAg",
      "text": "The 1970 treaty fell just short of a full legal recognition of the border since west Germany was not a sovereign country, only Germany as a whole together with the 4 occupation powers (France, UK, USA and USSR) could do so. Also Helmut Kohl's CDU / CSU was strongly opposed to the treaty while in opposition (also they were alligned with the Bund der Vertriebenen, the political arm of the displaced Germans from eastern Europe), so Poland in 1990 was all the more interested in Germany with them in power finally putting the border into a nationally and internationally legally binding form.\n\nThe legal tiptoying required for west Germany to even talk with east Germany was even worse.",

      "text": "Imagine Communism in the USSR and in Eastern Europe as a group of boulders perched along the bank of a river, in sight of the water, with the the bank representing the viability of the communist system and the river representing the free and wider world.       "text": "It's an interesting parallel to what Dr Paine was saying about the Soviet planned economy and their Continental mindset vs the western rules based order centered on free trade.       "id": "UgyG5IRoYIerf7v-LG54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I was born in Czechoslovakia 3 years before we were invaded in 1968. I was active member of student movement which brought down communism in our country in 1989. When I listen to this lecture I can attest that many things happened as described, yet you guys still don't get what it was like to live under communist regime under Kremlin leadership. We knew what was going on, at least if you lived in large city. We remember atrocities which happened under Stalin. We lived under heavy oppression, yet we had a great democratic traditions from 1918 to 1938 period so we knew that our regime is leading us into abyss, yet we had quite good education regardless of communism. There is one thing you should understand. To kick out Russian armies out of our land was quite an achievement. Generals were hostile and they used to say – \"We don't fucking care about your Gorbatchov, we are here to stay.\" When the last echelon left our country in 1991 it was almost a miracle, there is quite a tense story behind all this. It would be a long lecture to give you more reality about what it was like to live behind the Iron Curtain.",

    {
      "id": "UgyG5IRoYIerf7v-LG54AaABAg.AQydbNxhb-2ARwQl6bZKRC",
      "parent": "UgyG5IRoYIerf7v-LG54AaABAg.AQydbNxhb-2AQzM8WWsZs-",
      "text": " @DavidTeng-k7f  You can’t really compare the Austrian empire to the Soviet one. For example, the Czech lands within Austria were like Provence under France, actually in many ways in a better position - richer, with increasingly more independent organisation and with representation in the parliament. You wouldn’t say that “Provence was always controlled by someone: Rome, Paris…”. It’s the same for central Europe: just because Austria-Hungary was called an empire, it doesn’t mean it acted towards its constituents like the other empires. In fact, many of the central European states had their proud and long autonomous tradition and independent statehood. And the Czech lands within the Austrian empire were actually the richest part, except Vienna and Lower Austria, and they had most of the developed industry, highest literacy and flourishing civil society (from the second part of the 19th century). Whereas under Soviet control and communism, the Czech lands plunged from a wealthy and highly developed country to a backwater. We Czechs are very happy the Soviets are gone, and being voluntarily in the EU and NATO is a great benefit for us and we actively worked very hard to get into these voluntary organisations.",
      "like_count": 4,
      "author_id": "UCleM093Upz5HOE4wvw7G6Lg",
      "author": "@karelkieslich6772",

      "text": " @DavidTeng-k7f Comparing Austro-Hungary to the Soviet Union is quite far off. At the start of WW I, Hungary was already largely independent. And the Austrian-dominated rest might have evolved into something more federal had WW I not brought all peaceful attempts to a brutal halt.",

      "text": "I really like her lectures and analysis of history, which is quite a bit different angle than other historians.       "id": "UgyxyLnj1-U8RSZe6nN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "On the soviet work culture in the 1980s: \nMy grandmother said that in the early 1980s many would skip work to go shopping, catch up with friends etc. because there was 0 incentive to work (getting fired is almost impossible, paycheck is stable, promotion tied to years of experience and connections). It was heavily impacting the productivity. So, the government decided to crack down on it by sending police and kgb in civillian clothes to the malls, parks, restaurants. Those caught skipping work would get a fine or bribe the official into letting them go. \n\nMy father in law, started working at a factory in the 1990, at the age of 16. Often he would simply dip his hands into machine oil at the beginning of his shift (so that it looks like he was doing something) and then hangout with his friends who also worked at this factory for the rest of the day. Yet as his job was considered dangerous (heavy machinery with questionable reliability) he was making a salary of an average engineer.\n\nMy father grew up in a small mining town. There was no street lighting, but in the evening everyone walked with a flashlight. The same type. It couldn't be bought anywhere (legally), but was standard issue for the miners. Because miners got it for free and could always report it as lost in the mine and get a new one, they would sell them very cheaply (for a pack of cigarettes or couple of bottles of vodka).",
      "like_count": 553,
      "author_id": "UCY07nUWd1xP-80dAT9il_TQ",
      "author": "@9kaart",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/nxAP15v9oKt5_2MC0-Gzgu6wuyhgXo98LHZuCwuqkeQC-XkzdcRjoayqiFzSW6za2LkCwL3lLj8=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "3 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1768780800,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "parent": "UgyxyLnj1-U8RSZe6nN4AaABAg",
      "text": "My story is from a Soviet fighter pilot, “we would pretend to work, they would pretend to pay us.”",

      "parent": "UgyxyLnj1-U8RSZe6nN4AaABAg",
      "text": "Another point is that not only did Soviet workers have no incentive to work, they also often needed hours to find something to buy in the shops. Either hopping between shops or standing in rows, they had to leave work. Sometimes they would simply join a row in front of a shop because they concluded that something worthwhile was for sale. And when against all odds some fresh gabbages were in the shop that was the main dish for the next days.",

      "id": "UgyxyLnj1-U8RSZe6nN4AaABAg.AQyLFeK5HHxAS7nzQPk8pk",
      "parent": "UgyxyLnj1-U8RSZe6nN4AaABAg.AQyLFeK5HHxAR2KU8u-skP",
      "text": "​ @sebastianegger7560 , mine told me similar things as well, although not to this extent. \n\nA lot of common people in the German Democratic Republic (typically in the countryside) still became even more diligent and resourceful, because the failing economic and limited infrastructure meant they basically had to become craftspeople in every trade in order to keep their own properties from falling apart, and to maintain (or reach) a certain quality of life. \n\nBut still, for the majority of employees, jobs were fairly secure and the workload was manageable without having to bend over backwards. After the wall came down, a number of people failed to adapt to the new \"Western\" work culture, because they had never learnt to market themselves as employees or business people, or to treat their jobs as a place to perform as best as they could in order to be successful.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCIc72Qd9FjclMoZ7SsdMCgg",
      "author": "@honeybadger4245",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nTVsbvx3MHG0T0-z8A5_O4T2X9ZYpV6eDWfUOo0dUjPA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",

      "id": "UgyxyLnj1-U8RSZe6nN4AaABAg.AQyLFeK5HHxARJYCsuZgak",
      "parent": "UgyxyLnj1-U8RSZe6nN4AaABAg",
      "text": "There's an old Georgian (probably other Soviet states too) joke about the police stopping a man and asking where does he work.\n\"At a domino factory, I painted the dots on them.\"\n\"So why aren't you at work?\"\n\"Today we're printing the empty ones.\"",

      "author_id": "UCc-0JDeVH5pBpQIbOS-ELxg",
      "author": "@nickzardiashvili624",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l09ZacWY8gfcAk-7tfMOvcM0FSAgU9ZRO1a4hxlP4=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgyxyLnj1-U8RSZe6nN4AaABAg.AQyLFeK5HHxAR4OT3z0RQV",
      "parent": "UgyxyLnj1-U8RSZe6nN4AaABAg",
      "text": "Yes vodka was currency, for it you got anything. Barbed wire and rubber insulated cables from border guards. Tractor machinist doing works on field with kolkhos equipment. Parts for machinery. You name it. As all spare parts were so difficult to get then people who car had second car in spare parts stashed in garages. \nSame time with some goods there were surplus like T25 tractors. Father said that at some point sovhos had so many T25 tractors mechanics didn't repair these and went to scrap metal with clogged air filter. As same time metal plan was due to fulfil and tractors with clogged filter were sent off again.",

      "id": "UgzNkJNbANOehsHzHMB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I really like Sarah, but to call Helmut Kohl a talented leader is a stretch.\nHis PhD was of minor quality, his behaviour and his dialect as well as his abismal foreign language skills were subject of mockery. He received the nickname \"Birne\" (pear) from the German satire magazine \"Titanic\" because of the shape of his head. But all the ridicule he received didn't make him less corrupt, he even influenced the decision of how to roll out the internet infrastructure because his pal Leo Kirch with his media empire had urged him to not use fiber optics but copper cables instead - Kohl received some nice sum (alledgedly around 200000 Deutsche Mark) for this \"favour\". Yes, he is portrayed by some as the \"Unification Chancellor\" but, at least in my opinion, he could've hardly done anything to prevent that outcome. The foreign minister at the time, Friedrich Genscher, was as important for our unification as Helmut Kohl. \nAs I'm not a historian (I simply lived through all that as a German citizen who was no fan of Helmut Kohl) much of the above is up for debate, of course.",

      "text": "I was serving in Germany when all of this was occurring. I got there when the run up to Iraq began in the papers. Left after we took our chem and nuke weapons out.       "text": "What a great duo you two are Sarah Payne. You are one of the best academics I’ve ever come across on YouTube and Dwarkesh. You are extremely brilliant in ideas. Always love to see a new video. Please make more.",

    {
      "id": "UgwmSKUNeZrpbg_zSst4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I’m the one who had one of those heavy combusting TVs. Color, but still from the vacuum tube era. And because in the 90s my parents could not afford sh*t, this miracle of Soviet tech stayed with us way over its lifetime, and one day something inside of it went in flames. Not the best smell, to be honest.\n\nI think I would add one more factor  (or two) - the effect of Chornobyl disaster and the Armenian earthquake of 1988. The earthquake relief depleted the budgets significantly. And as for Chornobyl when the scale of the problem became clear people could not believe how much they were mistreated and lied to by their government. It happened on April 26, and by May 1 they were still downplaying the problem and even organized festivities in Kyiv, ffs. I think this was the moment when a lot of people completely lost faith in the credibility of the system.",
      "like_count": 29,
      "author_id": "UC1MF-iu3ucbh_vg8a2jwOHA",
      "author": "@ok_cfc",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n78rG8Jm5KURSTY-vpfJwwt9EghzksiCrDxokqzfiQ3ztb9lWOUyFcFSzM7c9eCldKxg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    },
    {
      "id": "UgwmSKUNeZrpbg_zSst4AaABAg.AQxaeGahYY7ARIJJdZy3vA",
      "parent": "UgwmSKUNeZrpbg_zSst4AaABAg",
      "text": "True the impact of Natural disaster are often brushed past in history analysis. And I think both these events showed that Soviet media/information control wasn’t what they believed it to be so they couldn’t play the old cover up game, the information was getting out",

      "text": "Saudi Arabia in my opinion doesn’t get enough credit for the collapse of the USSR, but of course it not just one country one president and they did a lot to fail themselves, and I’m not a huge fan of Saudi Arabia, but after the oil crisis they realized that was a big mistake and they really didn’t like the USSR because the USSR was anti religious and anti monarchy so they felt that the USSR was a large threat to them.       "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m5ztqa2lRI-V_3aj5ZJnAYak6wGfXgyrxRl68w_TEzS0s=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugy9mmUAUmwhQDDI3ad4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Were I wiser I would keep my mouth shut on this, but here's my thinking on how Gorbachev could have done reforms. \n\nHandle it in a manner somewhat similar to the British Empire's de-colonization. These places want you out, but that doesn't mean you need to lose your economic connection to them. Do increasing amounts of Glasnost (scaling them up as countries near independence on your terms), but threaten the leadership with the tanks unless you can keep economic ties and assurances. Then copy a lot of what they are doing. They have most of the same problems you do (because you're the one who inflicted them in the first place). Bring in the experts, the companies, ect. \n\nYou still have a great deal of potential power. You have incredible natural resources, you have nuclear weapons, you have population (for the most part), you have industry, and you have the fact that most nations don't want the U.S. to be the sole power of the world. You don't need to try and hold on to every last scrap of power and influence when your core system is dysfunctional.",

      "author_id": "UCBxhQMjF_okGNsEzF1kxGPg",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Professor Paine. I am a woman and when I am in the retirement home I don’t want to share a room with a man. You can if you like. I do not want to share a cell with a man. I do not want to share a hospital room with a man. I do not want to share a fitness changing room with a man. \n\nWe don’t have a flat tax cause we think a person who makes more should be taxed more on income over a certain point. Watch YouTube tax system explained in beer. The problem is not the collection of taxes, except property taxes in northern Illinois, it’s obscene. The problem is were the money is going. It is going to foreign countries, foreign entities and foreign nationals in far too great numbers. And as you have said we come, we dump billions, then leave and they still hate us. Are we insane? The boomers could work a part time job and pay for college. I could not, I am Gen X.  It has gotten so much worse for each generation. Universities get tax dollars per student, the state ones at least. They get tuition from students. The students get a guaranteed loan from government, sometimes a grant. The university gets tax money for research. They make money on that research. The university gets money from athletic programs, from alumnae, from gifts for foreign governments. So little money for an adversary to ruin a generation of American’s. How with all this money coming in has the cost of university education outpaced inflation? All they teach is to hate America. When I went we learned to think. We were instructed by our boomer teachers to always be skeptical and push back and don’t be rigid in thinking. Conservatives are more open minded and flexible than liberals today. Changed the definition of the word. It really should be a concern who uses which school bathroom and changing room. XX,XY. Science right there. Talk about an Emperor’s New Clothes moment. It is taking children to point out, but mommy, she is a man. He thinks he is female, teacher’s say he is female, some other kids going along with he is female, but he has male parts. She is a man. Tailor told the Emperor and the servants and people all reinforced this falsehood until a brave kid spoke truth.",

      "id": "Ugy-zlZVL3TZ7wcpqeJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Erich Honecker wasn't the \"tank man\". Not just because this titel is reserved for the man in the famous picture, but also because the east german military wasn't deployed in '53 or when the warsaw pact gunned down the prague spring. The National Peoples Army of the gdr had a command structure that required direct soviet orders to be deployed. The succsessor to Honecker was Egon Krenz who publicly congratulated the CCP how they handled their \"counter-revolutinary uprising\" and aides later said, that Krenz wanted to use the Army, but without soviet help and the lackluster bureucacy it couldn't happen. Honecker was more a friend with his chief for the secret police Erich Mielke and thought that the Stasi would fix this little unrest.\n\nHelmut Kohl ... well his career wasn't really impressive. A rumor that arose in the 80s has persisted to this day: Kohl’s dissertation, submitted in 1958, was allegedly so poor that it was removed from libraries on the orders of the federal government. He didn't even used headings and there are a lot of funny sentences like: “The Palatinate is home—so far as such general statements can be made—to a cheerful and cosmopolitan people who have a strong sense for social life and the pleasures of the times, and who are averse to dogmatic thinking.” Kohl wrote his phd only to put a Dr. (the german academic titel for phd = Doctor) in front of his name, which gives more prestige to someone in politics who didn't achived anything in life.\n\nWell how we get it taught in german schools and university and learn it in the media: Gorbatchow didn't really bothered about the reunification and that the whole of Germany would be part of NATO, because Gorbatchow didn't really saw a threat from NATO anymore. \n\nNo, the germans don't understand finance anymore. Rushing the fiscal union was horribly bad. The reunification lead to more than 25% out of a job and 10% leaving the new federal states. It was an economic disaster, especially if you compare it with the rebound both germanys had after the second world war or China experienced when they transformed to a market economy.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "@ 16:15 Toynbee's \"Civilzations die from suicide, not murder\" matches what I have long thought, that the Soviet Union died from socialism.  Socialism does not work.  Reagan's military buildup, US submarines, and all the other shocks hurried up the suicide, but did not murder the Soviet Union.\n\nDwarkesh's first interview question is why the Soviet Union lasted so long, and my answer is the same as has propped up every unpopular regime since time immemorial, whether dictatorships or democracies: regimes use outside threats, real or not, to distract the public from domestic troubles.  Stalin and Khrushchev were good at provoking Westerners into taking their bait and overreacting.  Bush Jr used Iraq and Osama bin Laden.  Obama used race.  Trump used (and uses) trade.  Biden used wokism.\n\nDuring the interview, Sarah discusses Russia needing a huge army to defend its borders while Britain only needed a small navy.  I have a book somewhere on this, maritime nations vs territorial nations.  Nations with land borders need permanent hierarchical armies, where top-down coordination is vital.  Maritime navies, on the other hand, during the age of sail, might not return for years, and this bred independent thinking, along with making armies smaller and less important.  Russia is the quintessential territorial nation with almost no border security.  Democracy may eventually come of age in Russia, but only after it has had stable land borders for a long long time, and Putin is doing his damnedest to delay that day of stability.",

      "id": "UgyrDMEZCQ5K19ftSvZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Question:\nI have often wondered why the collapse of the Soviet Union was relatively peaceful.\nThroughout its 60-year existence, the regime had no hesitation in using the military and secret police to enforce policies and maintain power both domestically and abroad. Given this history, why did these factions not attempt a military coup or uprising to preserve their authority?\n\nTo clarify, I am not suggesting that such an outcome would have been desirable. Rather, my impression has been that military dictatorships typically resist their demise forcefully rather than accepting it without significant conflict.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC0nQDI9GYPDGlovPR6MdAew",
      "author": "@obsidian53-B",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/xtok4DKwMG4bwIwObSl8DtWTdpZvfVsGHyqTxW9hvxt2IJ5nlX0C-u2l8M-E5P1EA64L8xDu=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "1:20:44 The problem was not the work schedule. There was no honest work for most people. There was no money, people returned to barter. Most of the economy didn't function. It's also strange to flex long hours when Russian have always worked longer hours than Americans.",

      "id": "UgxIyFCnmZs7qTQ6IC94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "1:20:38 Yeah, that optimism quickly turned into despair for most people. Nothing worked, bandits took over the country, financial system didn't function properly, almost no one had money. Deaths skyrocketed, birthrate plummeted (that effected is called \"Russian cross\" because it looks like it on a plot). Russians did get freedom to read and write whatever they wanted, travel anywhere, that's about one good thing about the '90s. There was no democracy, the same party leaders rebranded themselves as democrats and quickly fixed most elections.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCu_5qWC7lMl0yhySqrMwedA",
      "author": "@mpr1984",

      "id": "UgzHO0DSblQuwWcuDyl4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Tiananmen Square wasn't as unique as she thinks it was.  Czechoslovakia and Hungary already set the pattern of repression of democratic reforms by Communist regimes.  In both cases, they extended the lives of the regimes by decades.  China saw that the unwillingness of Poland, East Germany, and Hungary to stamp out grassroots democracy had led to the downfall of the regime.  So, in China, you had a political and economic system that was led by the survivors of the Cultural Revolution that had flourished under economic reforms, which was now faced with extinction by the same grassroots democracy that wrecked the Soviet Bloc.  If you asked any of the trigger men in China if they thought economic reform could succeed, while stifling democratic reform, they would be amazed at Tiananmen Square's long-lasting results.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCfJYCWK5nNU1F583uilqvOQ",
      "author": "@idsnowdog",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m5haELUg_NVNei9yPs334ar0tHeqoxdOyQwV17SEoZVwQwchwNuznoIBlsVGQpH9xupQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyyiR242tUz-UAehwx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I studied in the Soviet Union, Belarus and Russia, in 1988. The situation at the stores was not that bad at all, we even had decent meals at the student canteen. But, of course,  it didn't mean that the economy was in a good shape overall.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCc_AeIz1fQ3XCBQa76WB2nQ",
      "author": "@AKaczor2024",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_k489dbUjVHiavMXCVBLGMHjuZ1MbGhFgMATRJyE25ZAk1KhQl3s6Hf7REnBDXFhbKjBA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "timestamp": 1768780800,
      "is_pinned": false

      "id": "UgzU30pb76mCqo8nbXB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Soviet union is not russian federation",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCzOChi9dGHcTuR_PHnj-nSQ",
      "author": "@renanmonteirobarbosa8129",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n2lvTM102xEdKPBd7l06feyOnwYaaP4OLG8vjIBILRA8wB=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
