      "parent": "UgzU30pb76mCqo8nbXB4AaABAg",
      "text": "But they pretend to be. Every time they complain about nato going east, that is based on USSR deals.\nEvery time they claim they have authority over slavic nations, that is based on USSR. \nWhen they demand a seat at the table of power, they claim it based on USSR.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Dr. Paine appears to minimize President Reagan's impact, limiting her explanation of his contribution to his accelerating the arms race.       "id": "Ugw_5mXlqon3kdV6M294AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Kids, gather around. Let me tell you a story. In the late 1980s, a certain phenomenon was taking over the population in countries east of Berlin. Jeans. Do not get me wrong; Eastern countries produced their clothing as well. However, Levi's jeans were a highly priced commodity. Whoever got those jeans was boss. Girls will soon be able to differentiate between bosses and non-bosses. Wearing Western jeans significantly improved your night out each time. Now imagine, if you were in possession of seiko watch and Marlboro cigarettes. As limited as they were, you made sure not smoke them. You could be overweight 5'3\" lil douche, but those few items miraculously transformed you into a $ex machine. As a result, the boys became frustrated for not having any of those magical tools. Consequently, the girls grew frustrated, believing their boys were losers. And they met on the street protesting the government for destroying their lives. The lesson of the story is:  Each and every government should keep in mind that we are just weak humans with our ridiculous needs... This is how the mightiest nuclear-powered empires collapse...",

      "id": "UgxM0RJhW7oSf8Hjl6Z4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "To Sarah's point about conditions in the USSR, as one who came of age during the Cold War I was made aware of the \"Music School Effect\" so heavily deployed by the Soviets and their proxies. They identified extraordinarily talented people from an early age, primarily in the arts and athletics, and lavished scarce resources on developing them. The Kremlin and other Eastern Bloc governments would then use them as symbolic of the superiority of their societies vis-à-vis the decadent west. We all saw in the Olympics the prowess of the Soviet hockey team, East German swimmers, or Romanian gymnasts, but we weren't fooled into thinking these gifted people represented the average person in their countries. The vanguard of communist artistic and athletic excellence was merely a thin veneer concealing a thoroughly rotten system.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCT21hy2rtq0NvtV-ODwvpqw",
      "author": "@kchall5",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "1:41 interesting comments about the institutions. I have long felt that our short term free market views have destroyed our institutions and our ability to think strategically in the long term. I believe europe and the US, lacking the ideological threat of the soviet union, no longer needed to prove that our way was superior, they no longer needed to fear workers revolting and communism taking over.  \n\nThey could start reversing all those pesky regulations that we put in place after WW2. They could stam out labour movements, they could create extremely long supply chains going all over the world and move their factories easily to where it was cheaper and environmental regulations are not as strict (this is a cost we all must bear by the way, why don't we never count it?). \n\nThey could forget all about how people in the early 20th century turned to fascism when their economic systems failed to deliver growth for them. All those lessons forgotten because the generations who lived through WW2 died off.\n\nWe can for instance, directly trace the EUs shoddy electrical system (France excluded, Sweden too until the 1980s) of today to the free market reforms they have put in which have removed all the incitements for developing stable, long term power production. We forgot to treat electricity as a strategic resource and thought it was a market commodity (it's not and the system for making it into one is about as artificial as a command economy would be). Turning away from Russian gas has crippled european competitiveness for a generation. \n\nAs has our insistence on austerity instead of investment in our own economies and improving peoples purchasing power, for europe to be one big export oriented economy, we have to depress domestic wages. This has resulted in the EU falling behind the US by a lot since 2007 when we were equal. The over-reliance on markets and lack of strategic thinking has brought us here. Maybe finally it can end, maybe finally the EU will see the need of regular people to get some benefits too and not just the billionaires.",

    {
      "id": "Ugx5mTq5fhW38ShkXYx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Man, Sarah Paine is really good at making her lectures engaging and thought-provoking. I just wish my uni professors were the same.",
      "like_count": 94,
      "author_id": "UCIAAesSHBfHsETh9a8NsG3g",
      "author": "@Auvinius",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lmDFV3_UFIqZFoLdBbAoKxYfoS6Q8NhcgnzHnYwT3qAyU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

    },
    {
      "id": "Ugx5mTq5fhW38ShkXYx4AaABAg.AQvqmsSIDXnAQzu_1LRXHt",
      "parent": "Ugx5mTq5fhW38ShkXYx4AaABAg",
      "text": "I had pretty good profs in university, but presentations like Paine's would have been so useful in high school, where I did have a few good history teachers, but a lot of it was just, \"Memorize the dates and names for the test and done.\" I was thinking there would be an amazing demand/need for a simpler or more foundational version of these for younger kids (as these do not require but are certainly better with a base of knowledge).",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UC-zADqJFsJmhBVNv_wW7aKA",
      "author": "@brek5",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kh4raoDnX3ucrWDCA67SE_iOR590Ea97pR6vPYa0svTw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,

      "_time_text": "3 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1768780800,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugx5mTq5fhW38ShkXYx4AaABAg.AQvqmsSIDXnAQzwcWKt9j4",
      "parent": "Ugx5mTq5fhW38ShkXYx4AaABAg.AQvqmsSIDXnAQzu_1LRXHt",
      "text": "​@brek5 The memorization thing is so dumb. What you really need is to know the order in which things happen so you can look at them from cause-and-effect viewpoint. The exact dates themselves will become easier to remember with just repition. What makes history fun are the stories and insight it tells about us. I also had a good history teacher in high school, but he understood that asking about the dates is less important to being able to reflect on WHY things happened and what we should take away from those events. His only downside was being too easy in his grading. Otherwise a great guy.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCIAAesSHBfHsETh9a8NsG3g",
      "author": "@Auvinius",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lmDFV3_UFIqZFoLdBbAoKxYfoS6Q8NhcgnzHnYwT3qAyU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "_time_text": "3 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1768780800,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugx5mTq5fhW38ShkXYx4AaABAg.AQvqmsSIDXnAQzyx7Bzfuq",
      "parent": "Ugx5mTq5fhW38ShkXYx4AaABAg.AQvqmsSIDXnAQzwcWKt9j4",
      "text": " @Auvinius  Oh, for sure, those were teachers who were just dialing it in, and I knew it as a kid. My best teacher was one would would point us to stuff we could read outside of school, so the majority of my pre-university history knowledge was done on my own at the library and had nothing to do with school at all (and in university and afterwards, but I was much better prepared to study on my own by that point).\n\nBut I was a weird. self-motivated kid who would go to the public library in his free time and research stuff on my own, which was helpful in its own way, but I realize not all kids can or will do that (and obviously, I went down lots of less-than-productive routes compared to had I had more guidance). It would just be nice if kids could get exposed to this type of history at a younger age without having to go out and navigate it on their own, haha.",

      "text": "I would have chewed my right arm off to have been able to have her as a history professor ... along with Heather Cox Richardson and Joanne Freeman (\"What the heck just happened\" with the two of them on YouTube makes you realize that they've probably forgotten more about the Revolutionary and Civil War than most school districts' worth of teachers ever knew and can put every story and essay right on your grocery store shelf as to whay what happened then is important to understand what is happening today.)     {
      "id": "UgxthnNg9fZFvHpbLoR4AaABAg.AQvhJUrY5h4AQwTUgd6M4G",
      "parent": "UgxthnNg9fZFvHpbLoR4AaABAg",
      "text": "Ouch. Patel's role here is easy to overlook but it is important.\nFirst off, not every lecturer on a specific subject  neccessarily has the skillset to promote themselves on social media. Often the more specialized and academic in nature, the more this is true.  Paine doesnt really strike me as someone who is overly concerned with clout, surface style or media optics outside of professionalism.  She's ALL substance and while I find her deadpan sarcasm charming, and she IS likable, she doesnt strike me as a person who notices or cares too much whether people like her. \nFinding, vetting and \"selling\" people is also a skill, and in the world of social media, style method counts. Everything from the thumbnail and title presentation that frames your video, down  to the analytics. Ms Paine has spent a lifetime curating her knowlege in universities and libraries and even on the streets of Moscow, and presenting at the Naval Academy.  I dont think she wants or needs a PT job managing an independent media channel. Its a whole additional workload that would presumably be new to her. And while her focus is broad in terms of areas of society affected, she will be the first to admit her knowlege is of specific cultures and periods and currents, predominantly Russian and Japanese history and culture,  and their geopolitical relations with US, China and ec other, mostly from the interwar period through the end of the Cold War, as well as WW2 European theater as well. Patels channel includes other references that go beyond Ms. Paine's specific areas of expertise. \n   Also Patel asks open ended questions or questions  that, while they may seem uneccessary or sometimes backwards to us, they actually prod or nudge  Paine to explore and speak to the absolute limits of her expertise. Like any professor, she has her \"greatest hits\" that she reiterates and riffs on, sorta like a leitmotif in music. He asks her unexpected questions and Ive noticed this often engages her to explain things from a different angle than she did before. And while ppl sometimes accuse some of his questions of being odd or backwards, remember, he is trying to ask challenging questions.\n        Finally, as amazing as Ms. Paine is, she is of an older generation than many of, probably most of, Patels listeners. Im probably on the older end of audience and she is a generation older than I.  Sure those of us over 40 into WW2 history wouldve probably eventually stumbled across her if she was on her own channel. \n But Patel serves as an important cultural bridge to younger Millenials and Gen Z.  He reached, attracted and cultivated an audience, and it turns out for alot of us, she is our favorite among his channel \"topics\", and it seems as she becomes a \"regular\", they are growing the channels audience together now. \n   While I could listen to her lecture all night, Id also be very interested in Patel identifying other \"hidden gems\" of lecturers, academics,  policy wonks, geopolitical historians, sociologists, anthropologists, and political scientists and interviewing them or having them do a short lecture to start.",
      "like_count": 37,
      "author_id": "UCduiaza-DqjhYckJs1bSTpg",

      "text": " @DurrutiColumn  shes 68 and probably mostly retired from research.  youre right about the channel thing. Itd be hard to get non-teaching researchers to hold these lectures cause theyre basically rewritten books/articles. Theres a difference between teaching intro classes to non-professionals and presenting your research to an audience of postgrads. Shes able to do both of course, but the format doesnt work for a casual audience and for many there is a pridething in that as well.\n if youre interested, maybe check out these youtubers:\n-Prof James Ker-Lindsay\n-Metatron (his history stuff not the slop/drama stuff)\n-HistoryBuffs (if you like movies)",

## Description

This is the final episode of the Sarah Paine lecture series, and it’s probably my favorite one.

Sarah gives a “tour of the arguments” on what ultimately led to the Soviet Union’s collapse, diving into the role of the US, the Sino-Soviet border conflict, the oil bust, ethnic rebellions and even the Roman Catholic Church. As she points out, this is all particularly interesting as we find ourselves potentially at the beginning of another Cold War.

As we wrap up this lecture series, I want to take a moment to thank Sarah for doing this with me. It has been such a pleasure.

If you want more of her scholarship, I highly recommend checking out the books she’s written. You can find them here: https://www.amazon.com/stores/S.-C.-M.-Paine/author/B001HCVOTG

But would-be tank man Erich&nbsp;&nbsp; Honecker was already out of a job. His ruinous policies of living off debt since&nbsp;&nbsp; he came to power in 1971 had just about wrecked&nbsp; East Germany. So he was out. Then less than two&nbsp;&nbsp;

weeks later, the Council of Ministers resigns. Then on November 8th, the Politburo resigns.&nbsp; Then on the 9th, whatever is left of that&nbsp; government is issuing new travel regulations.&nbsp; You might wonder what travel has got&nbsp;

to do with it. I'll get there. So&nbsp;&nbsp; in response to a question at a news conference,&nbsp; this guy, Günter Schabowski, who was one of the&nbsp;&nbsp; remaining communists helping run the show, gets&nbsp; asked a question and he doesn't know the answer.&nbsp;&nbsp;

So he wings it. The question is, "When do these&nbsp; travel regulations go into effect?" And he goes,&nbsp;&nbsp; "Immediately." Well, crowds immediately started&nbsp; gathering at the six gates to the Berlin Wall.&nbsp; At one of them, the border guards decided&nbsp;

that discretion was the better part of valor,&nbsp;&nbsp; and they opened the gate and East&nbsp; Germans poured into West Berlin.&nbsp; Within the first week alone, over half of&nbsp; East Germany's population visited the West.&nbsp;

Within the month, 1% of the&nbsp; population emigrated to the West.&nbsp; Like the Polish elections, this opening&nbsp; of the gate was a pivotal decision.&nbsp; A pivotal decision, whatever it is, means&nbsp;

there's no going back to the way it was.&nbsp; Here's good old Günter going, "Gosh, we&nbsp; hadn't a clue that opening the wall was&nbsp;&nbsp; the beginning of the end of East Germany."&nbsp; Okay, better luck next time. And the Russians&nbsp;&nbsp;

were shocked by how unpopular they were. They were thinking they were going to get credit,&nbsp;&nbsp; Gorbachev, for Eastern Europe's liberation rather&nbsp; than blame for Eastern Europe's enserfment.&nbsp; Here you have Yuri Ryzhov, a scientist&nbsp;

and parliamentarian going, "All of our&nbsp;&nbsp; former satellites by compulsion cast off&nbsp; from us as fast and as far as possible."&nbsp; And Anatoly Kovalev, who is a deputy foreign&nbsp; minister, said, "Look, we had no confidence&nbsp;&nbsp;

whatsoever concerning whom the East German army&nbsp; is going to shoot, the demonstrators or us.&nbsp; And the same thing for the Polish and&nbsp; Hungarian armies." Great. With allies&nbsp;&nbsp; like this, who needs enemies?

The allies kind of cover it.&nbsp; So this argument says unrest in the empire forced&nbsp; the Soviet Union to forfeit the Cold War. Okay,&nbsp;&nbsp; I got another counterargument.&nbsp; It says, "Nonsense, the real&nbsp;&nbsp;

problem was that the satellites were unhealthy. That's why the whole thing fell apart. So this map&nbsp;&nbsp; is 1960. You see all those tempting green places. They're about to become independent, and they are&nbsp;&nbsp; really sick of their Western European colonizers.

Enter the Soviet Union with a program to put the&nbsp;&nbsp; West out of business. There were&nbsp; many takers. Fast forward to late&nbsp;&nbsp; 1980s. The Soviet Union is on a roll. Small hitch, in the late 1970s there&nbsp;&nbsp;

was a big recession that continued into&nbsp; the 80s and tanked commodity prices.&nbsp; For some of the newfound pals like Angola,&nbsp; South Yemen, Ethiopia, Nicaragua, it wrecked&nbsp;&nbsp; their export earnings because they're exporting&nbsp;

commodities and these commodity prices are down.&nbsp; In many cases, it halved them. The Soviet Union was really&nbsp;&nbsp; dependent on oil exports, still is. Oil prices tanked and oil accounted&nbsp;&nbsp;

for up to 55% of the Soviet budget. So here Brezhnev has got a deep bench&nbsp;&nbsp; of non-performing piles at a time when he&nbsp; doesn't have the money to support all of them.&nbsp; Worse yet from the Soviet point of view,&nbsp;

it's dumped all this money in these Third&nbsp;&nbsp; World friends but meanwhile, it's got its&nbsp; own nationalities who are deeply unhappy&nbsp;&nbsp; and they want out of the empire. Most problematically, they all&nbsp;&nbsp;

revolt at exactly the same time. One of the rules for continental&nbsp;&nbsp; empire is "no two-front wars". Russia has so many fronts at&nbsp;&nbsp; this point, it can't even keep count.

The unrest in the internal empire of&nbsp;&nbsp; nationalities started as soon as Gorbachev got in. There were student movements in Kazakhstan and&nbsp;&nbsp; Yakutia, opposite ends of things. By the time you get to 1990,&nbsp;&nbsp;

there are like 76 seething ethnic&nbsp; rebellions in different parts of this.&nbsp; There was too much going on for&nbsp; the Soviet government to handle.&nbsp; So you could argue that the Soviet Union&nbsp;

bankrupted itself with the Third World while&nbsp;&nbsp; ignoring its own internal Third World&nbsp; of nationalities, whose simultaneous&nbsp;&nbsp; revolts brought down the Soviet Union. I got a completely different argument for you.&nbsp;

If you don't like all of those, I got&nbsp; another one for you. It's the economy,&nbsp;&nbsp; stupid, right? That line. One could argue&nbsp; that communism failed as an economic system.&nbsp; If you look at growth statistics for&nbsp;

the Soviet Union, they're pretty good&nbsp;&nbsp; post-World War II when they're rebuilding, but&nbsp; they really stagnate from the mid-70s onward.&nbsp; For the decade preceding Gorbachev’s coming&nbsp; to power, Soviet growth stats were one to&nbsp;&nbsp;

two percent lower than those of the United States,&nbsp; and the compounding effects of that were enormous.&nbsp;&nbsp; What's going on? Everyone's lying to each other.&nbsp; The data that Soviets are using is garbage.&nbsp; If you're working for a subunit of an enterprise,&nbsp;

you have to lie about the inventories you have,&nbsp;&nbsp; saying you have less than you do, and&nbsp; then you have to lie about what you need,&nbsp;&nbsp; saying you need more than you do because&nbsp; you're worried about getting enough things.&nbsp;

It's not a market system&nbsp; where the price dictates it.&nbsp; This is all about the plan. You've got to enter the right numbers&nbsp;&nbsp; and then you get whatever inputs you get from the&nbsp;

centralized plan. So everyone's lying. They're&nbsp;&nbsp; aggregating all the lies. The higher up the food&nbsp; chain you aggregate these things, the worse the&nbsp;&nbsp; data is, so that the Soviet government has no idea&nbsp; what the actual value of capital or labor are.&nbsp;

It has no idea what actual productivity is, and&nbsp; no one has any idea what consumer preferences are.&nbsp; You're not using markets and prices. The misallocation of capital and&nbsp;&nbsp; labor goes unnoticed until it&nbsp;

metastasizes into a catastrophe.&nbsp; To give you a sense of these misallocations, the&nbsp; Soviet Union was rotting 20 to 40% of its crops.&nbsp; It's using scarce hard currency for agricultural&nbsp; imports to make up for those crops, a total mess.&nbsp;

You can look at what happens to&nbsp; the economy with oil prices down.&nbsp; We're into a spiraling mess, so that from&nbsp; when Gorbachev comes in in '85 to when it&nbsp;&nbsp; hits a trough in Russia in 1998, you see this&nbsp;

crashing share of world GDP by the Eastern bloc.&nbsp; If you look at Soviet statistics on deficits,&nbsp; trade balances, debt, they're just soaring,&nbsp;&nbsp; and then GNP growth goes double-digit negative.&nbsp; That's called shrinkage. It's not the normal&nbsp;&nbsp;

thing. Marshall Yazov, here's his take: "We simply&nbsp; lack the power of all these wealthy NATO nations.&nbsp; We had to find an alternative to the arms race." And here's a foreign service officer,&nbsp;&nbsp; Anatoly Adamishin.

He said, "Look, our problems began&nbsp;&nbsp; with the departure from isolation. The main reasons for collapse&nbsp;&nbsp; were internal, not external reasons. The Soviet economy was literally exhausted from&nbsp;&nbsp;

this monstrous arms race, militarism, enemies with&nbsp; half the world." That's his take. Gorbachev told&nbsp;&nbsp; the Central Committee, "Look, we're encircled not&nbsp; by invincible armies, but by superior economies."&nbsp; He often told people, "Living this&nbsp;

way any longer is impossible."&nbsp; So you can make a powerful argument that it's&nbsp; the Soviet economy that lost the Cold War.&nbsp; This gentleman, Alexis de Tocqueville, is&nbsp; very famous for writing a book about the&nbsp;&nbsp;

last days of the French monarchy before&nbsp; the French Revolution overturned it.&nbsp; He also wrote something about Democracy&nbsp; in America, both excellent books.&nbsp; But this one's from the one about France, where&nbsp;

Tocqueville observes, "The most dangerous moment&nbsp;&nbsp; for a bad government is when it begins to reform." Russians of all political persuasions&nbsp;&nbsp; agree on at least one thing. That is that Gorbachev's role in&nbsp;&nbsp;

how the Cold War turned out was pivotal,&nbsp; that he played a very essential part.&nbsp; Gorbachev made his decision based&nbsp; on certain false assumptions.&nbsp; One of them was the irreversible&nbsp;

direction of history.&nbsp; Gorbachev thought of history going always forward&nbsp; towards communism, never backwards to capitalism.&nbsp; Of course, Eastern Europe took a U-turn,&nbsp; went straight back to capitalism.&nbsp;

Here is Leonid Shebarshin, who is a senior&nbsp; person in the KGB, their intelligence office.&nbsp; He said, "The thought never occurred&nbsp; to the government that it's possible&nbsp;&nbsp; to withdraw from socialism."

If you think about both communist&nbsp;&nbsp; theory and how imperialism works in practice,&nbsp; usually the mother country is more developed&nbsp;&nbsp; than whatever all the colonies are, right? Well, the Soviet Union was an inverted empire.&nbsp;

People in Eastern Europe as a group were more&nbsp; well-educated and they were richer than Russians.&nbsp; It was like a donut empire. So when the empire went to Eastern Europe,&nbsp;&nbsp; Russians could no longer siphon off the wealth&nbsp;

of these enserfed populations in Eastern Europe,&nbsp;&nbsp; which explains why they wanted to leave. It also suggests why Putin wants them back.&nbsp; Another false assumption has to do&nbsp; with the sentiments of the neighbors.&nbsp;

Gorbachev was convinced he was going to&nbsp; get credit for liberating Eastern Europe,&nbsp;&nbsp; rather than blame as a Russian for&nbsp; having enserfed them in the first place.&nbsp; For Gorbachev, the clock began on his watch.

For other people, no, Stalin's when it began,&nbsp;&nbsp; when he started shooting a lot of people. Here you have Anatoly Chernyaev,&nbsp;&nbsp; foreign policy adviser to Gorbachev, saying&nbsp; that Gorbachev thought that bringing freedom&nbsp;&nbsp;

to our Eastern European satellites would&nbsp; have them adopt socialism with a human face.&nbsp;&nbsp; "He made an enormous mistake because these&nbsp; countries brutally turned their back on us."&nbsp; Really, if that's brutal, then&nbsp;

what pray tell was Stalin?&nbsp; And then it gets better: "The politics in&nbsp; connection with our former friends were&nbsp;&nbsp; totally unexpected to us." Really?&nbsp; You occupy people, you never leave,&nbsp;&nbsp;

you shoot a lot of people in their&nbsp; government, you put in a new government,&nbsp;&nbsp; you siphon off a lot of their wealth, and&nbsp; you impose a non-performing economic system,&nbsp;&nbsp; and you wonder why they don't like you. Think&nbsp;

about the United States. It intervenes all&nbsp;&nbsp; around the world in other people's troubles. It dumps billions in economic aid and even&nbsp;&nbsp; leaves and people don't like us. I don't know why the Russians&nbsp;&nbsp;

think they're so special. Another false assumption:&nbsp;&nbsp; Gorbachev believed that if the Warsaw Pact,&nbsp; the military alliance of the Eastern Bloc,&nbsp;&nbsp; disappeared, then NATO would disappear.

He also believed that if the Comecon,&nbsp;&nbsp; which is their trading organization, went away,&nbsp; then the European Community in those days—it&nbsp;&nbsp; becomes the European Union later—would disappear.&nbsp; Not quite. It turns out that organizations that&nbsp;&nbsp;

are coercive versus those that are voluntary,&nbsp; they dissolve for different reasons.&nbsp; And then Gorbachev also assumed that the United&nbsp; States would share a continental outlook of not&nbsp;&nbsp; wanting strong powers and that the United&nbsp;

States therefore would not want a unified&nbsp;&nbsp; Germany, let alone a strong unified Germany. So when all the unrest is happening in Germany,&nbsp;&nbsp; Gorbachev is off taking a vacation. Poor life choice, because at that moment,&nbsp;&nbsp;

President George Bush Sr. and Chancellor Kohl&nbsp; of Germany are working on fast-tracking German&nbsp;&nbsp; unification of a fully sovereign,&nbsp; unified Germany—both halves in NATO.&nbsp; So many of Gorbachev's closest supporters&nbsp;

at the end of it all blamed him.&nbsp; They said, "Look, his foreign policy mistakes were&nbsp; a function of his domestic policy mistakes and it&nbsp;&nbsp; destroyed the Soviet Union." Back to this America expert,&nbsp;&nbsp;

Vladimir Lukin: "Gorbachev was no Deng Xiaoping." And Arbatov, who's their premier America expert:&nbsp;&nbsp; "The stupidity of our leaders caused&nbsp; the disintegration of the Soviet Union."&nbsp; So the big bozo was playing with plastic&nbsp;

bags, stuck one on his head, committed&nbsp;&nbsp; suicide. It was by mistake. Lukin continued:&nbsp; "In the West, they love Gorbachev because&nbsp;&nbsp; everything took place so easily and cheaply,&nbsp; basically like that, but only for you. For us,&nbsp;&nbsp;

it was expensive." But you could argue the time to&nbsp; reassess all the Stalinist stuff was long overdue.&nbsp; Here's a completely different&nbsp; way of looking at it.&nbsp; I've been giving you sins of commission, and now&nbsp;

I'm going to do sins of omission. It's a good&nbsp;&nbsp; framework. It's useful for other things. The sins&nbsp; of commission are all the things Gorbachev did.&nbsp; Now what I'm going to do&nbsp; is what the army didn't do.&nbsp;

Some would argue that the Red Army&nbsp; should have done exactly what Deng&nbsp;&nbsp; Xiaoping ordered his army to do. You just send the tanks against&nbsp;&nbsp; civilian demonstrators and they&nbsp;

truly crush them and it'll be over.&nbsp; Communist Party is still in&nbsp; power in China 30 years later.&nbsp; So there are some people who believe&nbsp; that this was a terrible mistake.&nbsp;

So this argument would be that&nbsp; timely tank deployments—TTD,&nbsp;&nbsp; my contribution to military acronyms—would&nbsp; have changed the outcome of the Cold War.&nbsp; Others would be back to the great men&nbsp;

of history and sins of commission,&nbsp;&nbsp; and they wouldn't be picking on Gorbachev&nbsp; but his successor Boris Yeltsin.&nbsp; There are two big pieces of evidence when we look. He removed Article 6 from the Soviet Constitution,&nbsp;&nbsp;

which guaranteed that the Communist&nbsp; Party would always monopolize power.&nbsp; And then in addition in the following&nbsp; year, Yeltsin's the head of Russia,&nbsp;&nbsp; he gets together with the heads of Ukraine and&nbsp;

Belarus, and they signed the Belavezha Accords,&nbsp;&nbsp; which then formally dissolved the Soviet Union. So according to this way of thinking,&nbsp;&nbsp; it's his fault. It's suicide on purpose. And&nbsp; what it does is it opens the door for multiple&nbsp;&nbsp;

parties and for the nationalities within&nbsp; the Soviet Empire to become independent.&nbsp; So I've given you internal explanations.&nbsp; I've given you external explanations. Now I'm&nbsp;&nbsp; going to give you some umbrella explanations.

They're based on all the preceding evidence,&nbsp;&nbsp; and they come to opposite conclusions. The first one was, well,&nbsp;&nbsp; any of the above, it's inevitable. The opposite conclusion from the same evidence is&nbsp;&nbsp;

that no, it took all of the above. The West barely&nbsp; won. I'm going to start with "any of the above".&nbsp; You could argue with this many serious&nbsp; problems, it was a matter of time&nbsp;&nbsp; before the Soviet Union collapsed.

It was an objectionable system for&nbsp;&nbsp; precisely the reasons the West didn't like it. It had a brutally inefficient economic system.&nbsp; Russians who invented the thing, at the&nbsp; end of the day, didn't want it either.&nbsp;

By this way of looking at it, you have people like&nbsp; Yuri Ryzhov, a genuine rocket scientist, who says,&nbsp;&nbsp; "Look, the main reason for the collapse of the&nbsp; Soviet Union is the rottenness of its system."&nbsp; Then here's a journalist, Teimuraz Stepanov, who&nbsp;

said, "Look, I think from the beginning the genes&nbsp;&nbsp; of disintegration were contained in the genetics&nbsp; of this governmental political formation."&nbsp; Don't you love the products of&nbsp; the Soviet educational system?&nbsp;

Don't ever use wording like that. So you could argue that the Soviet Union&nbsp;&nbsp; was destined to fail with this many problems. Others would come to the opposite conclusion.&nbsp; They would say, "No, it took every single one of&nbsp;

them for the Cold War to end on Western terms."&nbsp; Back to Anatoly Kovalev, the deputy&nbsp; foreign minister, he said, "Look,&nbsp;&nbsp; all these factors merge—internal, ideological,&nbsp; economic, military—it's all of them.&nbsp;

You remove any one of them and&nbsp; you get a different outcome.&nbsp; Maybe the Cold War ends, but it&nbsp; might end completely differently."&nbsp; So by this line of reasoning, the West barely&nbsp;

won and should feel very fortunate that it did.&nbsp; One can take this last argument&nbsp; and say it was more than that.&nbsp; It also took the confluence in&nbsp; office of two very talented leaders:&nbsp;&nbsp;

Helmut Kohl of Germany and George Bush Sr. of&nbsp; the United States, not the son who got into&nbsp;&nbsp; those forever wars, but the dad who didn't. George Bush Sr. had one of the most amazing&nbsp;&nbsp; resumes of any person ever to become president&nbsp;

of the United States. Just look at him. When he's&nbsp;&nbsp; really young, he's a war hero in World War II. He's a Navy pilot, a dangerous thing to do.&nbsp;&nbsp; He did it. Then he comes back and he gets&nbsp; his BA at Yale and graduates with honors.&nbsp;

Then he becomes a representative for this district&nbsp; in Texas after he's already made himself a&nbsp;&nbsp; millionaire in the oil business that he started. Then he became ambassador to the UN,&nbsp;&nbsp; followed by US representative to the PRC,&nbsp;

before we had formal diplomatic relations.&nbsp; So he's the guy who's setting that up. He becomes director of the CIA, and then&nbsp;&nbsp; he is Ronald Reagan's understudy&nbsp; for eight years as vice president.&nbsp;

He is incredibly fit for the job. Helmut Kohl is equally fit for the job.&nbsp; He is the longest-serving chancellor&nbsp; in German history since his illustrious&nbsp;&nbsp; predecessor, Otto von Bismarck.

He starts out getting a PhD in&nbsp;&nbsp; history and political science. He also starts out in business,&nbsp;&nbsp; but then he works for state government, initially&nbsp; as a representative, then as a governor.&nbsp;

He becomes chairman of his political&nbsp; party, the Christian Democratic Union,&nbsp;&nbsp; for a quarter of a century. Once he gets in, he decides&nbsp;&nbsp; he's going to buy up East Germany one&nbsp;

tourist at a time. How does that work? East&nbsp;&nbsp; Germans, it turns out, really like to travel. West Germans had always been able to travel to&nbsp;&nbsp; East Germany, or they long had been able to travel&nbsp; to East Germany, but East Germans definitely could&nbsp;&nbsp;

not easily travel to West Germany. Why?&nbsp; Because they have a habit of staying.&nbsp; But all of a sudden, East Germany&nbsp; eases up on the travel regulations.&nbsp; You might ask why, and the answer would be money.

Just like the Poles, the East Germans were deep in&nbsp;&nbsp; an economic mess of their own making. Would-be tank man Erich Honecker,&nbsp;&nbsp; who got the boot at the very end, well, his&nbsp; staying-in-power paradigm that he implements&nbsp;&nbsp;

in 1971 is that he's going to live off debt. He needs to make certain social benefits&nbsp;&nbsp; available and consumer benefits available for&nbsp; labor stability, to not have labor unrest.&nbsp; The way he's going to do that is he's not going&nbsp;

to do many domestic investments and he's going to&nbsp;&nbsp; do a lot of borrowing, particularly from&nbsp; West Germany. Well, that's unsustainable&nbsp;&nbsp; long-term. By the time you get to the end of&nbsp; the Cold War, if he's going to fix that and&nbsp;&nbsp;

even out the accounts, it would be a 30%&nbsp; decline in the East German standard of living.&nbsp; So he really needs the pocket&nbsp; change from the tourists.&nbsp; So what Kohl does is a brisk&nbsp;

business of tourists and things.&nbsp; What he does in return for the&nbsp; easing of travel restrictions,&nbsp;&nbsp; he pays East Germany several hundred million&nbsp;&nbsp; Deutschmarks extra to allow that to happen.

And then he gets the Hungarians to go along.&nbsp; He gets the Hungarians to open up their Austrian&nbsp; border to let East Germans out that way,&nbsp;&nbsp; and he gives them a half a billion&nbsp; Deutschmarks for that little favor.&nbsp;

When Kohl introduces his 10-point unification&nbsp; program—because now he's thinking he's going&nbsp;&nbsp; to get both Germanys together—this is when he&nbsp; starts doling out big bucks to the Soviet Union,&nbsp;&nbsp; whose economy is unraveling.

Gorbachev is going to be&nbsp;&nbsp; desperate for this cash as that's happening. So West Germany provides 100 million in food,&nbsp;&nbsp; especially in meat, for the Soviet&nbsp; Union that doesn't have these things.&nbsp;

Nevertheless, the unrest just keeps on going. The Berlin Wall, as I've told you, is breached,&nbsp;&nbsp; and then you wind up with a West German&nbsp; caretaker government, and the financial&nbsp;&nbsp; situation in Russia itself is unraveling.

By the time you get to January 1990, Bush and Kohl&nbsp;&nbsp; get together and they decide they want to really&nbsp; fast-track German reunification. Why? Because&nbsp;&nbsp; they've got to get it done before this unraveling&nbsp; crisis causes Gorbachev to fall from power.&nbsp;

So they have got a game going, the&nbsp; two of them. It's complicated. Here's&nbsp;&nbsp; why. Gorbachev was dead-set against&nbsp; Germany, a united Germany, in NATO.&nbsp; He's not really keen about a united&nbsp;

Germany, let alone one in NATO.&nbsp; The US State Department experts, the guys&nbsp; who know everything, are saying, "No,&nbsp;&nbsp; you want to go slow on this unification business." Kohl is also running a coalition government.&nbsp;

There are people in that government he cannot fire&nbsp; because they're from different political parties.&nbsp; One of them is his foreign minister,&nbsp; this guy Genscher, who is very skeptical&nbsp;&nbsp; about Germany being part of NATO.

Then it turns out, although Britain&nbsp;&nbsp; had talked a good piece during the Cold War,&nbsp; it didn't actually want a unified Germany,&nbsp;&nbsp; nor did France. Why? Because that unified&nbsp; Germany would eclipse them economically.&nbsp;

They didn't want that to happen. So Kohl and Bush divide up the tasks.&nbsp; Kohl is going to reassure the Soviet&nbsp; Union that Germany is not going to&nbsp;&nbsp; be belligerent or do horrible things.

And Kohl is going to work on financial&nbsp;&nbsp; unification because the Soviets are&nbsp; thinking in terms of military unification.&nbsp; You know, where you deploy your troops.&nbsp; That determines things. Wrong instrument&nbsp;&nbsp;

of national power, precisely because&nbsp; the Soviets didn't understand finance.&nbsp; That's why they're in such a mess. Whereas the&nbsp; Germans do. What they're going to do is get East&nbsp;&nbsp; Germany on the West German Deutschmark,&nbsp;

and at that point they will control all&nbsp;&nbsp; the money and they will control decisions. But the Russians aren't going to see that coming.&nbsp; Meanwhile, Bush is supposed to work the alliances&nbsp; particularly with Britain and France in the West.&nbsp;

There are all sorts of&nbsp; meetings that are coming up.&nbsp; Bush's job is to delay those meetings for&nbsp; as long as possible so German unification&nbsp;&nbsp; can proceed as far as possible.

The two of them are doing a tag-team&nbsp;&nbsp; diplomacy with Gorbachev that he just can't&nbsp; keep up with, given that his own home economy&nbsp;&nbsp; has got these double-digit shrinkage rates.&nbsp; Here's how they go. As the trades get bigger,&nbsp;&nbsp;

the amount of money you pay Gorbachev gets bigger. First of all, it's just to get a unified Germany.&nbsp; Then it's to get a unified Germany&nbsp; with West Germany still in NATO.&nbsp; Then it's to get a unified Germany&nbsp;

with all of Germany in NATO.&nbsp; So here's how the money goes. Gorbachev agrees&nbsp; to German unification. We are no longer paying&nbsp;&nbsp; hundreds of millions of Deutschmarks. We're paying billions of Deutschmarks,&nbsp;&nbsp;

five billion Deutschmarks for that one. Then Gorbachev agrees that states can choose their&nbsp;&nbsp; own alliances, i.e. whether or not to join NATO. The US offers nine assurances, but it's also a&nbsp;&nbsp; trade agreement that Gorbachev really wants.

Then the economic union goes into effect.&nbsp; So we've now done the financial&nbsp; reunification of Germany.&nbsp; This is when there's a London Declaration&nbsp; that's inviting Eastern European countries&nbsp;&nbsp;

to coordinate more closely with NATO. In return, Gorbachev gets a promise&nbsp;&nbsp; of a G7 summit meeting that's going to&nbsp; fast-track aid to him, which it will do.&nbsp; And then Gorbachev agrees&nbsp;

to German NATO membership.&nbsp; At this point, even bigger things are happening. Germany's going to agree to its border with&nbsp;&nbsp; Poland. I'll get there and explain. Germany&nbsp; provides 15 billion in Deutschmarks,&nbsp;&nbsp;

including building all kinds of new apartment&nbsp; buildings for repatriated Soviet soldiers who are&nbsp;&nbsp; going home. Why are you doing that? Because you&nbsp; want those soldiers focused on buying furniture,&nbsp;&nbsp; not running a military coup. That's what they're&nbsp;

doing. So the unification happens in mid-September&nbsp;&nbsp; 1990. Here's the Polish borders. At the end of&nbsp; World War II, Stalin moved Poland 200 kilometers&nbsp;&nbsp; to the west, and it winds up taking a third of&nbsp; German territory by the time that's all over.&nbsp;

So the Germans don't really&nbsp; want to sign all that away.&nbsp; In addition, as part of that, there were 12&nbsp; million German refugees who were thrown out&nbsp;&nbsp; of wherever they were living to send them&nbsp;

back to Germany, of whom 2 million died.&nbsp; So this is a big deal and it's in living memory. Germany agrees to this, that the borders are&nbsp;&nbsp; done. German-Polish borders are set. Complicating&nbsp; factor: a month and a half before this unification&nbsp;&nbsp;

treaty is signed, Saddam Hussein decides he's&nbsp; going to invade Kuwait because he's broke.&nbsp; He's had a long war with Iran, huge debts, many&nbsp; owed to Kuwait, which he doesn't want to pay back.&nbsp; So if you invade them, that solves that problem.

Also, he would take over Kuwait's very rich&nbsp;&nbsp; oil fields, and together that would make&nbsp; Iraq probably the swing producer of oil.&nbsp; So he thinks that's a great idea. Except the Cold War's over actually.&nbsp;

The Russians are more than willing&nbsp; to cooperate with the United States.&nbsp; Gorbachev really needs more money, and he&nbsp; is willing to go along with getting Iraq out&nbsp;&nbsp; of Kuwait, but not with regime change in Iraq.

Because think about it, Iraq is a very important&nbsp;&nbsp; debtor state to the Soviet Union. It owed them between $10–13 billion.&nbsp; That's a lot of money for a broke creditor. But Gorbachev is being extraordinarily&nbsp;&nbsp;

cooperative with Bush Sr. He sends Yevgeny Primakov on&nbsp;&nbsp; multiple missions to Baghdad. The first one, Primakov&nbsp;&nbsp; gets all Russian hostages out of Iraq.

Then on the second trip, he gets all Westerners&nbsp;&nbsp; out, Americans included. Third trip, not so&nbsp; lucky. He's there for the coalition force bombing.&nbsp; I don't think he liked that very much. But imagine that bombing going on if&nbsp;&nbsp;

there were Western human shields&nbsp; going down with every target.&nbsp; Russia took that card right off the table. Here's&nbsp; some of the reasoning. Sergei Tarasenko was an&nbsp;&nbsp; aide to Foreign Minister Shevardnadze, and they&nbsp;

understood that the United States was going to&nbsp;&nbsp; do something about this invasion of Kuwait. So the Russians thought, "It'll be better&nbsp;&nbsp; if we force all of this to go through&nbsp; the UN, where Russia has a veto power."&nbsp;

He said, "Look, there was a division of roles." It extends to China, the help that Russia&nbsp;&nbsp; provided. "When the Americans&nbsp; asked us to work with the Chinese,&nbsp;&nbsp; we told the Chinese, 'Think about it.

You're one of the big five with veto power.&nbsp; Doesn't it suit your interest to funnel everything&nbsp; through the UN where you can put your foot down?'&nbsp;&nbsp; And the Chinese came around to that idea." However, the Russians had red lines.&nbsp;

Here's Anatoly Kovalev again,&nbsp; the deputy foreign minister.&nbsp; The red line is, American troops stay out of Iraq.&nbsp; No regime change in Iraq. You do that and you will&nbsp;&nbsp; tank the termination of the Cold War.

And that would be the goal.&nbsp; Here's Kovalev saying, "I advanced the&nbsp; basic principle that we must support the&nbsp;&nbsp; territorial integrity of Iraq. This was our sacred&nbsp; position. We must not permit a division of Iraq."&nbsp;

So if you wonder why the ground war&nbsp; ended after 100 hours, this is it.&nbsp; The big thing out there is war termination of the&nbsp; Cold War. That's the big thing. Saddam Hussein is&nbsp;&nbsp; a minor event over there. Sorry, but he was.&nbsp;

If it had tanked Cold War termination or upset&nbsp;&nbsp; the reunification of Germany, France&nbsp; and Britain might have been very happy,&nbsp;&nbsp; because François Mitterrand, who is the president&nbsp; of France, and Margaret Thatcher, prime minister&nbsp;&nbsp;

of Britain, were against German unification. They knew it would marginalize their own country.&nbsp; Germany's going to be a&nbsp; bigger economy, which it is.&nbsp; François Mitterrand eventually found solace&nbsp;

in expanding the European Community to the&nbsp;&nbsp; European Union when you're incorporating&nbsp; all these Eastern Bloc countries into it.&nbsp; He plays a really important role in concluding the&nbsp; Maastricht Treaty that forms the European Union.&nbsp;

But Margaret Thatcher just plain lost. She was just upset about the whole thing.&nbsp; She said, "Germany will be the Japan&nbsp; of Europe and worse than Japan."&nbsp; I guess she hadn't been to Japan lately.

She said, "The Germans will get in peace&nbsp;&nbsp; what Hitler couldn't get in war." She wanted to leave Red Army troops&nbsp;&nbsp; in Germany for the duration. Imagine if that had been the&nbsp;&nbsp;

case and now dealing with Putin… If he had&nbsp; troops in Germany, we would be in trouble.&nbsp; But Bush and Kohl worked around all of them. Bush said to Kohl at the end of it, "Look,&nbsp;&nbsp; I'm not going to beat my chest&nbsp;

you now owe us to fix everything. The counterargument to that is,&nbsp;&nbsp; "No you are an enormous migraine. You set back all of these countries&nbsp;&nbsp; across the globe in time with this nonfunctioning&nbsp;

administration, that if we dumped a lot of money&nbsp; in it, it would just go straight into corruption.&nbsp; You need a legal structure in order to place&nbsp; money, and they just plain didn't have it.&nbsp; That was another thing that was&nbsp;

worrying the Bush administration.&nbsp; There's nowhere to put the money. Speaking of these different countries that&nbsp;&nbsp; the Soviets and the United States were competing&nbsp; for during the Cold War, you had this presentation&nbsp;&nbsp;

where you say Reagan alone didn't do this. But I wonder if the broader lesson is that&nbsp;&nbsp; nothing any US president did in terms of&nbsp; foreign policy… That was all a sideshow,&nbsp;&nbsp; this tête-à-tête competition for different Third&nbsp;

World countries: "We're going to get Brazil, we're&nbsp;&nbsp; going to get Vietnam, we're going to get Algeria." That just seems much less significant than the&nbsp;&nbsp; fact that liberal capitalism was more&nbsp; appealing and out-produced communism.&nbsp;

So even if some country, even if Brazil&nbsp; goes communist, this is not going to change&nbsp;&nbsp; the fundamental playing board here. If you do not protect the liberal economies&nbsp;&nbsp; of Europe, you're not going to have anywhere to&nbsp;

play the liberal economic game, and also Japan.&nbsp; One of the reasons you feel that liberal&nbsp; economies work is you've got economic&nbsp;&nbsp; miracles going on in Japan, Korea, Taiwan,&nbsp; Singapore, and Hong Kong back in the day.&nbsp;

So if you abandon those places... Also in the Cold War, there was a&nbsp;&nbsp; tremendous amount of economic growth across&nbsp; the world, particularly in the Third World.&nbsp;&nbsp; Why? Because in the past, if there's a civil&nbsp;

war, whoever's losing either comes to us or&nbsp;&nbsp; comes to the Russians and says, "Help us." So whoever it is helps, and then the other&nbsp;&nbsp; side feels obliged to help, and then you're&nbsp; just destroying wealth ever more rapidly.&nbsp;

The Cold War was anything&nbsp; but cold in the Third World.&nbsp; Tens of millions of people&nbsp; died in these conflicts.&nbsp; So when you end that, all of a sudden&nbsp;

they can start compounding growth.&nbsp; So there is a problem with not&nbsp; countering someone who's going&nbsp;&nbsp; to impose communist systems all over the place.&nbsp; Communist systems are really&nbsp;

good at putting dictators into&nbsp;&nbsp; power in a civil war situation. It's very&nbsp; effective. That's how Mao gets into power.&nbsp; The problem is, then they win&nbsp; the civil war, they're in power,&nbsp;&nbsp;

they annihilate the opposition, but then&nbsp; it produces compounding poverty thereafter.&nbsp; So there is this conundrum, and I&nbsp; genuinely don't know the answer to this.&nbsp; In order to beat off these communist factions&nbsp;

and guerrillas, we often through the Cold War&nbsp;&nbsp; had to support other dictators. Probably in many cases they were&nbsp;&nbsp; better than the communist alternative. It's just very hard to beat Pol Pot&nbsp;&nbsp;

and Mao in terms of how terrible you can be. But obviously this was in its own way problematic.&nbsp; Even if we didn't have to support&nbsp; dictators, we had to alienate countries.&nbsp; You had this previous lecture that you gave&nbsp;

on the Indo-Pakistani chapter in history where&nbsp;&nbsp; we had to alienate India in order to fend off&nbsp; against the Soviet Union in this little episode.&nbsp; I don't know what the solution to this is. If you think that this theater mattered less, then&nbsp;&nbsp;

you could say we should have just kept our hands&nbsp; clean of these different Third World countries.&nbsp; But to your point, if you want to be able to&nbsp; show that these countries are going to experience&nbsp;&nbsp; growth under capitalism, then you want them&nbsp;

to not be under the subjugation of communists.&nbsp; But then you have to support&nbsp; sometimes objectionable regimes.&nbsp; I think you had a more optimistic&nbsp; generation, ironically, optimistic.&nbsp;

The people who had survived World&nbsp; War II, there was a real generosity.&nbsp; American servicemen and women were welcomed&nbsp; all over Europe and they were adored in Europe.&nbsp; They came back and they were a very&nbsp;

generous group of people. Others felt&nbsp;&nbsp; generous to them. That's when the GI Bill&nbsp; just passed saying, "You've saved everyone.&nbsp; Therefore we're going to give you college&nbsp; educations, extend home loans to you."&nbsp;

Not to African Americans, they were&nbsp; excluded from this, which is a problem. But&nbsp;&nbsp; white Americans weren’t. It led to massive&nbsp; economic growth where people who'd never had&nbsp;&nbsp; a college education in their family, they did.

All of a sudden, instead of having really&nbsp;&nbsp; hard manual labor, this real optimism. And then it extended to foreign countries.&nbsp; This is when this country was tremendously&nbsp; generous to others, and it worked very well for&nbsp;&nbsp;

us. Think about the Marshall Plan. It looks really&nbsp; generous putting all this money into Europe.&nbsp; We made a fortune off of it, as did Europe. If you're smart, you're looking for win-wins&nbsp;&nbsp; of things where you both benefit because&nbsp;

that'll incentivize the other side to join&nbsp;&nbsp; in. This is basic strategy. This is one&nbsp; of the reasons I've got problems with the&nbsp;&nbsp; United States' turn to zero-sum approaches where&nbsp; "I'm going to get everything, you get nothing.&nbsp;

Then I look so smart when we do the clickbait on&nbsp; this moment where I get everything and you get&nbsp;&nbsp; nothing." It's much smarter. The other piece is&nbsp; that a lot of things don't pay off immediately.&nbsp; George Bush is not reelected president. He&nbsp;

absolutely deserved to be. Because what he did,&nbsp;&nbsp; the payoff was huge, ending&nbsp; the Cold War on Western terms.&nbsp; But it doesn't pay off in&nbsp; time for the next election.&nbsp;

I think this is where Americans miss it. You're looking at what someone does on&nbsp;&nbsp; a given day when the real implications&nbsp; are what's going to happen in a decade.&nbsp; Like on tax policy, if we keep racking up our&nbsp;

debt, it may get us out of the corner today,&nbsp;&nbsp; but is it going to back us into a corner later on? This is where Americans need to think a little&nbsp;&nbsp; harder about long-term implications of things. I thought when you pointed out that it would&nbsp;&nbsp;

cost 60 billion Deutschmarks for West Germany&nbsp; to pay Gorbachev to let East Germany join West&nbsp;&nbsp; Germany. That's a lot of money. But if you&nbsp; think about decades and decades of future&nbsp;&nbsp; growth, it's a huge bargain.

It's a mistake to think about&nbsp;&nbsp; how expensive things seem at the moment. It's another huge country that you've turned.&nbsp; There's a statement that politicians&nbsp; think of the next election,&nbsp;&nbsp;

statesmen think of the next generation. George Bush and Helmut Kohl are statesmen.&nbsp; They're thinking of the next generation. The group that fought World War II, many of&nbsp;&nbsp; US and allied leaders, were statespeople.

They're thinking of the next generation.&nbsp; Or if you're thinking of where I've&nbsp; got Mitterrand, who's negotiating the&nbsp;&nbsp; Maastricht Treaty about the European Union,&nbsp; that is statesperson's work of what's the&nbsp;&nbsp;

next generation. It's important. We need more&nbsp; statesmen, statespeople, political leaders.&nbsp; To try out a different thesis on you, through this&nbsp; period the Soviet Union is also trying to buy off&nbsp;&nbsp; other countries, especially when&nbsp;

it thinks its economy can grow.&nbsp; Especially when oil, after the 1973&nbsp; oil crisis, oil prices just skyrocket.&nbsp; This is why some Soviet citizens&nbsp; remember the Brezhnev era favorably.&nbsp;

Oil made it possible for the Soviets to not&nbsp; only import stuff, but through the Brezhnev&nbsp;&nbsp; period there's actually a net export of&nbsp; resources to Eastern European satellites&nbsp;&nbsp; rather than the other way around.

That's probably their data. I get it,&nbsp;&nbsp; their oil is really subsidized, but&nbsp; everything in the Soviet Union that was&nbsp;&nbsp; worth having came from somewhere else. The problem is how do you measure it?&nbsp;

They're just going to measure&nbsp; by weight or something else.&nbsp; It doesn't really capture what they're getting. The larger question being that, it's not like&nbsp;&nbsp; the Soviet Union didn't think of&nbsp;

doing things like the Marshall Plan.&nbsp; Obviously nothing to that extent, but this idea&nbsp; that you can win people's favors by providing&nbsp;&nbsp; them military aid, providing them foreign aid. They just didn't have the resources to do it to&nbsp;&nbsp;

the extent that the US could. That's true,&nbsp;&nbsp; but there's a real coercive piece too. If you mess with them, it'll be really ugly.&nbsp; Here's what I don't understand about&nbsp;

the arms buildup during the Cold War.&nbsp; The Soviet Union is spending 2% of their GDP&nbsp; just on nuclear weapons alone at its peak.&nbsp; Arms control advocates will make this quip,&nbsp; which is that we've already got enough weapons to&nbsp;&nbsp;

destroy the world many times over. Why do we need&nbsp; more? But that is sort of an interesting question.&nbsp; What was the point of spending so much&nbsp; of GDP on the marginal nuclear weapon&nbsp;&nbsp; or marginal weapon system?

I don't know the answer,&nbsp;&nbsp; but you read the plans about these things&nbsp; and you wonder what people are thinking.&nbsp; We were trying to develop tactical nukes. There was only a little trick with that.&nbsp;

Whoever deployed it would be within&nbsp; the blast range of the tactical nuke.&nbsp; You're going, "Who develops a weapon like that?"&nbsp; Apparently we did. Luckily we didn't deploy it.&nbsp;&nbsp; I don't know the answer of why we&nbsp;

had such massive redundancy in these&nbsp;&nbsp; nuclear weapons, why the arsenals were so massive. I don't know the story on how you maintain these&nbsp;&nbsp; things and how long they last. It doesn't make much more&nbsp;&nbsp;

sense to me than it does to you. Another question. Sino-Soviet split,&nbsp;&nbsp; this huge diplomatic coup. The Soviets had to put a million&nbsp;&nbsp; soldiers on the Siberian front against China.

They had to spend 2% of GDP just stationing and&nbsp;&nbsp; garrisoning this area, which is obviously a lot. That's often what many countries spend on defense&nbsp;&nbsp; as a whole, let alone just along one front. At the same time, 2% GDP, well if they just&nbsp;&nbsp;

had one or two more years of extra&nbsp; economic growth or faster growth,&nbsp;&nbsp; that could make up for this huge diplomatic coup. Again this goes back to the point of, if some&nbsp;&nbsp; domestic policy just caused slightly higher&nbsp;

economic growth rates, that would make up for the&nbsp;&nbsp; biggest diplomatic coup of the entire Cold War. It goes back to economy first, diplomacy second.&nbsp; Firstly, I have real problems with the statistics. I got a sample size of one, moi. I remember living&nbsp;&nbsp;

in Moscow. It was so backwards.&nbsp; It's just breathtakingly backwards&nbsp;&nbsp; in just about every way imaginable. They got a big fancy subway system that looks&nbsp;&nbsp; remarkably retro, and at least it works.

But the consumer goods were so awful,&nbsp;&nbsp; the quality was so bad. You look at the buildings themselves.&nbsp; I get it, they make nuclear weapons. Do they&nbsp; make anything else? Their cars were a joke,&nbsp;&nbsp;

their Ladas or whatever they were. It's just&nbsp; thing after thing. So you're looking at all&nbsp;&nbsp; their stats because that's what they&nbsp; are telling you, that we're so great.&nbsp; It really is an Emperor Wears No Clothes&nbsp;

moment that finally the little kid goes,&nbsp;&nbsp; "Oh, you're actually naked." I can give you an example.&nbsp; These acquaintances in Moscow were&nbsp; talking about hospitals outside of Moscow&nbsp;&nbsp;

that some of them didn't have running water. How do you have a hospital without running water?&nbsp; I don't even know how that's even conceivable. Or when their kid had put her hand through a&nbsp;&nbsp; glass door or something.

They wanted to get her&nbsp;&nbsp; stitched up because she's bleeding. She’s not going to die, but she's&nbsp;&nbsp; probably bleeding all over the place. They bring her to one place and, oh,&nbsp;&nbsp;

they got no thread to do the stitches. So then they have to go to another place.&nbsp; Who runs a country like this? Alright, you convinced me. BART&nbsp;&nbsp; is acceptable. I'll stick here. Subway's not&nbsp;

a big deal. I don't want to move to Moscow.&nbsp; Okay, while the Eastern European satellites&nbsp; are trying to leave the Soviet Union, this has&nbsp;&nbsp; happened many times through the 20th century. Hungary in 1956, Czechoslovakia in '68,&nbsp;&nbsp;

Poland through Solidarity. Every previous time there's a&nbsp;&nbsp; many-million-person-strong Red Army stationed&nbsp; in Eastern Europe left over from World War II,&nbsp;&nbsp; which rolls in the tanks and prevents&nbsp;

these revolutions from taking place.&nbsp; So what happens in the late 80s and early 90s? The Red Army is still there.&nbsp; There's still millions of Red Army&nbsp; soldiers. They just don't shoot.&nbsp;

Generational change. The leaders&nbsp; don't have the stomach for it anymore.&nbsp; I don't know how you'd feel about&nbsp; sending tanks and going, "Oh,&nbsp;&nbsp; we're going to splatter all these people."

I think for many Americans, that would not&nbsp;&nbsp; be the choice that they would make. So this ruthless generation is gone.&nbsp; Another piece is that Gorbachev had traveled&nbsp; and I think he had some Czech friends.&nbsp;

I can't remember all of his lists of friends. But they'd been horrified by Czechoslovakia in&nbsp;&nbsp; 1968 as young people watching, as Russian&nbsp; young people watching it and thinking,&nbsp;&nbsp; "It's just wrong. We shouldn't be doing this.&nbsp;

If communism is what it should be, this is not&nbsp;&nbsp; what should be happening." This is of their youth.&nbsp; Gorbachev and his generation. It's not just him,&nbsp;&nbsp; he reflects a whole generation of communists. They're thinking, "There's got to be another&nbsp;&nbsp;

way. This is just not right." So&nbsp; he thinks he's got his other way.&nbsp; It's this exuberance of the reforms and&nbsp; things that are happening in Russia.&nbsp; There's a tremendous feeling of energy.

He's telling the Poles, "You get at it too.&nbsp; We're all going to do this thing." But it's all the expertise and things&nbsp;&nbsp; that he's missing, that he's unaware that&nbsp; he's missing, as are all these other people,&nbsp;&nbsp;

because how could they have it? They've been living in a command economy.&nbsp; This is what I wanted to ask you about. You had the de Tocqueville quote about&nbsp;&nbsp; how revolutions happen when governments start&nbsp;

to institute some kind of reform. Gorbachev&nbsp;&nbsp; is doing perestroika, glasnost. There's&nbsp; the conservative reactionary parts of&nbsp;&nbsp; the Communist Party, which by the way is&nbsp; a phrase I wouldn't expect to have said.&nbsp;

But they're trying to resist this. So Gorbachev goes about dismantling the&nbsp;&nbsp; party secretariat and instead devolving power&nbsp; down to the individual republics. We know what&nbsp;&nbsp; happens later. These republics are saying, "Look,&nbsp;

we want our own country now." But this raises a&nbsp;&nbsp; question. If you do inherit a brutal regime,&nbsp; and now you say, "I want to do reforms."&nbsp; You know this dynamic that de Tocqueville pointed&nbsp; out, which is that as soon as you start reforms,&nbsp;&nbsp;

actually what tends to happen is that you lose&nbsp; power, not that people consolidate it under you.&nbsp;&nbsp; What actually should you do? Because you're&nbsp; like, "I want to improve people's lives."&nbsp; But as soon as you try to do that,&nbsp;

the whole thing's going to fall apart.&nbsp; This is so far above my&nbsp; pay grade. I'm a professor.&nbsp;&nbsp; I have trouble justifying a B+ on a paper. I'm a believer in gradual reforms. Do it&nbsp;&nbsp;

incrementally. For the Soviet Union, it&nbsp; would be gradual legal reforms, work it&nbsp;&nbsp; through their Duma slowly, and do it that way. But seek out help from the European Union that&nbsp;&nbsp; has many, many experts that would&nbsp;

be overjoyed if Putin and friends&nbsp;&nbsp; would cease doing their number on Ukraine. Now the problem is you're going to get into&nbsp;&nbsp; reparations for the horrors they've inflicted. So that ship has sadly sailed for this generation.&nbsp;

There's no nice ending for Russians.&nbsp; It's too late. But you can look at&nbsp;&nbsp; Europe itself improving its institutions&nbsp; and Ukraine improving its institutions.&nbsp; If you think about what forces you to&nbsp;

change, the existential threat on Ukraine,&nbsp;&nbsp; if they survive all this, this is forcing&nbsp; them really to clean up their institutions.&nbsp; So it's happening rapidly there, but we don't&nbsp; know the end of that story, how it ends.&nbsp;

I do think these are interesting lessons here of&nbsp; whenever we look at a country from the outside,&nbsp;&nbsp; we have this thing of, "Well, just reform&nbsp; everything and just fix your economy."&nbsp; Whenever we understand the&nbsp;

system better… For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; in the United States, healthcare is 20% of GDP. This idea that Trump or Obama or Biden, whoever,&nbsp;&nbsp; could just come in and be like,&nbsp; "Well, I'll just fix healthcare."&nbsp;

We recognize that this is a wildly&nbsp; implausible thing to happen.&nbsp; But then we have this expectation that in Russia,&nbsp; Gorbachev or Yeltsin could have just been like,&nbsp;&nbsp; "100% of my economy is messed up,&nbsp;

and I'm just going to fix it."&nbsp; American hubris in action. Think about our&nbsp; country. We have one of the most crazy tax codes&nbsp;&nbsp; on the planet, and neither party can touch it. Because you touch any part of it,&nbsp;&nbsp;

someone negotiated that wording exactly. Yet think of how much of our economy is&nbsp;&nbsp; taken up by the overhead of all the&nbsp; tax accountants, all the misdirected&nbsp;&nbsp; cash in order to take advantage of something&nbsp;

that's simply an invention of the tax system.&nbsp; There was years ago when there was talk of doing a&nbsp; flat tax, "Wouldn't that be much more efficient?"&nbsp; You can imagine what accountants thought&nbsp; about that one. That idea has totally died.&nbsp;&nbsp;

Talk about inefficiency. Then we realize&nbsp; we have budgetary problems in this country.&nbsp; This would seem to be something that ought to&nbsp; be on people's radar, clean up the tax code.&nbsp; But isn't it precisely that many people&nbsp;

don't want the radar on the tax code?&nbsp; That's why we're wondering who can get in and out&nbsp; of girls' or boys' bathrooms, instead of looking&nbsp;&nbsp; at the tax code, which should be the real thing. I think there should be big&nbsp;&nbsp;

deductions for podcasts. It should count for research and development.&nbsp; Well, Dwarkesh, you're almost at that stage. You need to add a lobbyist in DC.&nbsp; We'll work on it. There's a very interesting&nbsp;

book about North Korea, I forget the title,&nbsp;&nbsp; where the author is pointing out that&nbsp; North Korea could not even start doing&nbsp;&nbsp; reforms today because as soon as there was some&nbsp; sort of information from the outside world that&nbsp;&nbsp;

North Koreans could see—which would be part of&nbsp; any reform—they would immediately realize that&nbsp;&nbsp; everything the government has told them is false. South Korea is enormously wealthier and they&nbsp;&nbsp; have this terrible standard of living.

Obviously, this is the same experience&nbsp;&nbsp; that Eastern Europeans had. Literally in many cases, you had a&nbsp;&nbsp; country that was bisected in half and&nbsp; the other half is living so much richer.&nbsp;

In those situations, I guess this goes back to&nbsp; the question of, "Well, today in North Korea,&nbsp;&nbsp; how would it even kick off if Kim&nbsp; Jong-un just had a change of heart&nbsp;&nbsp; or if somebody else came into power?"

They're probably just trapped in this to&nbsp;&nbsp; the extent that they want to keep power. Oh, he's trapped because he's a dead boy&nbsp;&nbsp; if he tries to take a go at retirement. In Asia—I don't know exactly all of the&nbsp;&nbsp;

parts of Asia where this applies to,&nbsp; it's some parts—there's a thought that&nbsp;&nbsp; things last for three generations and then&nbsp; it's over. So he's the third generation.&nbsp;&nbsp; Whether this is true or not doesn't matter.

If you believe it's true, it will become a&nbsp;&nbsp; self-fulfilling prophecy. So I'll be interested.&nbsp; I probably won't live to see it, you in the&nbsp;&nbsp; room will, what happens to the Kim family,&nbsp; whether it makes it to generation four or not.&nbsp;

But by their own belief system, in&nbsp; theory, they shouldn't. So who knows?&nbsp; One more question about oil. Based on my big expertise on oil, zero. Okay.&nbsp; During this period between '73 and '85,&nbsp;

when they had these huge oil revenues,&nbsp;&nbsp; presumably there was some amount of exuberance. But did the government recognize and realize that&nbsp;&nbsp; they're super fragile to the price of oil&nbsp; and if that collapses, they need some sort&nbsp;&nbsp;

of contingency plan, some rainy day fund? You must notice that, "Oh, this is half my&nbsp;&nbsp; budget, and all of my foreign currency&nbsp; is coming from oil, and this is a very&nbsp;&nbsp; volatile commodity." Nobody noticed that?

Yeah, well, it's interesting. I was reading&nbsp;&nbsp; this long chronology that was put&nbsp; together sort of like early Putin.&nbsp; So before they really shut&nbsp; down all the information.&nbsp;

It was just a chronology of&nbsp; the Cold War, big fat book.&nbsp; Just like someone like me&nbsp; to read a book like that.&nbsp; So I'm going date after&nbsp;

date after date after date.&nbsp; It's written by people who are really&nbsp; angry about how the Cold War turned out.&nbsp; One of the takeaways from the compilers&nbsp; of this thing is they kept criticizing.&nbsp;

They showed how much for every year&nbsp; Russia was making in oil revenues.&nbsp;&nbsp; It was huge. But in their analysis it&nbsp; was, "And they saved none of it", right?&nbsp; There was no sense of investing in something.&nbsp;

There's something called consumption. There's&nbsp;&nbsp; another thing called investment. Going around and&nbsp; buying a bunch of Western grain is consumption.&nbsp; There's none of this being put in&nbsp; anything that's going to yield anything.&nbsp;

So that was a big criticism&nbsp; from the authors of this book.&nbsp; To the question you're asking, "No, they&nbsp; just milked it while they were there."&nbsp; Final question, this is not so&nbsp;

much a question as an observation.&nbsp; I don't know if you have a reaction to this.&nbsp; Just look at Russia's history through&nbsp; the 20th century: tsarism, communism,&nbsp;&nbsp; collectivization, to more than 10% of&nbsp;

your population dying from World War II,&nbsp;&nbsp; then back to Stalin, and then more communism, and&nbsp; then the economy collapses again, and then Putin.&nbsp; Especially if you look at the satellite states,&nbsp; they had all of this happen to them and worse&nbsp;&nbsp;

because now they're getting invaded. Whereas you&nbsp; have other countries. Japan and Germany also had&nbsp;&nbsp; tragic histories, but then they recovered. Maybe it’s just the tragedy of Russia.&nbsp; Yeah, you're lucky you're not Russian.

Yeah, exactly.&nbsp; No, it is tragic. It is tragic. It started out as&nbsp; a difficult address, pre-Industrial Revolution,&nbsp;&nbsp; that required certain things to survive. They were more ruthless than their neighbors.&nbsp;&nbsp;

They did survive. I mean, in a previous&nbsp; lecture, I discussed how they wiped out&nbsp;&nbsp; entire princely states and Khanates&nbsp; and things, they just wiped them out.&nbsp; Then you're using their elites&nbsp;

because it's a rough neighborhood.&nbsp; The problem is if you aren't on the winning side,&nbsp; you're going to be on the losing side, right?&nbsp; But since the Industrial Revolution, where you&nbsp; can do compounded economic growth that comes&nbsp;&nbsp;

from commerce and trade and industry and things,&nbsp; that's the real way to get powerful because power&nbsp;&nbsp; becomes a function of your wealth. That involves having legal systems,&nbsp;&nbsp; institutions, and stability.

Russia has found it very difficult&nbsp;&nbsp; getting with that program. It has to do with, I think,&nbsp;&nbsp; this very difficult historical legacy of who&nbsp; rises to power, and also all the missing things.&nbsp;

They didn't have the Renaissance, they didn't have&nbsp; the Reformation, these fundamental movements that&nbsp;&nbsp; were very influential in the West. So there's a lot of negative space&nbsp;&nbsp; of things that didn't happen.

There's all the awful stuff that&nbsp;&nbsp; you saw that did happen, but then they're&nbsp; missing things. So it's very difficult.&nbsp;&nbsp; Then people like Putin can set the clock way&nbsp; back because he's killed so many Ukrainians.&nbsp;

What he's done will take a generation&nbsp; at minimum to get to anywhere where&nbsp;&nbsp; people are going to be thinking about…&nbsp; People will be talking about reparations&nbsp;&nbsp; from Russia for quite a while and they're&nbsp;

poor, they're not going to want to do that.&nbsp; I should have thought to end on&nbsp; a more optimistic note, but...&nbsp; Well, history's ended, okay? Well, you've outlined the ways in which&nbsp;&nbsp;

countries can chart a better course for themselves&nbsp; and that's where the optimism can come from.&nbsp; Actually, I've told a story about the last Cold&nbsp; War that stayed cold in the industrialized world,&nbsp;&nbsp; which was a good thing, because&nbsp;

it could have been nuclear.&nbsp; It was tragic in many other parts&nbsp; of the world, but at least it stayed&nbsp;&nbsp; cold in the industrialized part. There was a strategy that a very&nbsp;&nbsp;

thoughtful generation of people, not just&nbsp; in the United States but all over the West,&nbsp;&nbsp; put together to allow for a non-nuclear landing&nbsp; for the Soviet Union when it fell apart.&nbsp; From this, you can derive some of the&nbsp;

strategies that worked for ending it that way.&nbsp; These are the kind of strategies&nbsp; that we're going to have to use&nbsp;&nbsp; in order to navigate the second Cold War. The other piece about the Cold War is the Soviet&nbsp;&nbsp;

Union living miserable lives of their own making. But Americans were actually having a good time.&nbsp; They paid taxes, they had to&nbsp; pay for all the nuclear weapons.&nbsp; But as I recall, people are running&nbsp;

around in Disneyland, they're doing&nbsp;&nbsp; their European trips, they're buying houses. So actually Americans, people in Western Europe,&nbsp;&nbsp; were living fulfilling lives while they're&nbsp; waiting out for others to get with the program.&nbsp;

If we're going to make it through this second&nbsp; one, we need to start cooperating with our allies,&nbsp;&nbsp; building institutions, and improving laws. Don't just burn down the house.&nbsp; We will get through this one too, and we will&nbsp;

live fulfilling lives while we're waiting for&nbsp;&nbsp; Putin to come up with something different or&nbsp; Xi Jinping to come up with something different.&nbsp; But if we blow through our good hand of cards... You interview all kinds of people&nbsp;&nbsp;

at the cutting edge of technology. If we get rid of all of our university funding,&nbsp;&nbsp; we aren't going to have the intellectual&nbsp; capital on which those businesses are based.&nbsp; If we're going to dump all our allies for&nbsp;

unknown reasons and just alienate them so&nbsp;&nbsp; they organize without us… If we're going to just&nbsp; throw away entire institutions without thinking&nbsp;&nbsp; very carefully about what we're doing… We become&nbsp; a cooperative adversary and we will be the bozo&nbsp;&nbsp;

putting a plastic bag on our own head. I look at the rhymes here.&nbsp; The Soviets had this ancient leadership who just&nbsp; couldn't get their act together and they're living&nbsp;&nbsp; off of debt instead of thinking creatively.

The rhymes are awful, but we don't&nbsp;&nbsp; have to do it that way. So it is more optimistic,&nbsp;&nbsp; but we need to get our house in order. That's why I'm doing these lectures.&nbsp;

They're lectures in strategy to give&nbsp; you tools on how to come to your own&nbsp;&nbsp; decisions. That's your business, not mine. That is an excellent note to close on.&nbsp; Sarah, I want to thank you so much&nbsp;

for doing this lecture series with us.&nbsp; It has been a true education across these six&nbsp; lectures, everything from individual wars to the&nbsp;&nbsp; strategic and tactical decisions which explain&nbsp; them, to the broader lessons for today's world.&nbsp;

I do interview lots of different&nbsp; kinds of people, but from a sort&nbsp;&nbsp; of view-per-minute average-adjusted&nbsp; basis, I host a Sarah Paine podcast.&nbsp; If you just sort by popular,&nbsp;

Sarah Paine comes up a lot.&nbsp; But you've got it backwards. I was&nbsp; an unknown academic and then you&nbsp;&nbsp; cold-called me about doing an interview. I said,&nbsp;&nbsp; "Sure." Dwarkesh, as a result of all this,&nbsp;

> Brilliant lecture by Sarah Paine, but it’s a narrative designed to soothe the American ego rather than explain the cold reality of history. If you look at it from the perspective of those who actually lived it, the story isn't one of Western "victory," but of strategic betrayal:
> 
>     The USSR wasn't defeated; it was surrendered: Paine credits Reagan’s pressure, but the Soviet Union was a self-sufficient fortress. It collapsed because Gorbachev was naive enough to believe in a "Common European Home." He handed over the keys to the empire expecting partnership. Instead of a handshake, the West gave Russia the shock therapy of the 90s and pushed NATO to its doorstep despite every verbal assurance.
> 
>     The Helsinki "Trojan Horse": We celebrate human rights, but from the Russian side, Helsinki was the first experiment in "color revolutions." It wasn't about ethics; it was a weapon used to dismantle a sovereign state from within. What Paine calls "liberation," the Russian people experienced as a 40% drop in GDP, a collapse in life expectancy, and the rise of oligarchs mentored by Western economists.
> 
>     A Mirror for Modern America: Paine warns about the USSR’s internal rot, debt, and ideological blindness. The irony is palpable. While we lecture the world on the "death of the Soviet system," the U.S. is currently repeating the same mistakes: massive over-leverage, crumbling domestic infrastructure, and an obsession with exporting a brand of "democracy" that creates more chaos than stability.
> 
> The Soviet Union died of imperial overstretch and a crisis of faith. By celebrating our "victory" instead of analyzing our failures in the post-1991 settlement, we have turned a potential partner into a permanent adversary. Triumphalism isn't history—it's propaganda.

When I see Trump waving his finger, I see the worlds dominant super power that is essential to everyone else' existence trying to get it's allies in line, not lose them. 
>

The people wanted not only freedom from Moscow but more importantly freedom from their terrible governments. The people wanted freedom, democracy and capitalism. 
> 
> They wanted free and fair elections, freedom of speech, prosperity (meaning capitalism), environment protection, amnesty for political prisoners... freedom from Moscow was one of the things but that was much more considered automantic. Getting rid of the Czechoslovakian communist government included cutting ties with Moscow and joining the West, but getting rid of the Czechoslovakian communist government was the main goal. 
> 
> The sign in the centre of the picture (17:07) says "Down with the rule/government of batons". And they meant the Czechoslovakian government, not the Soviet government.  Batons were used by police against the demonstrating people so it was also demand for freedom of gathering specifically  and end of the use of violence to repress the people generally.  
> 
> 'Havel to the Castle' was one of the most common slogans of the demonstrations - Václav Havel was the most known disident who was in prison at the time and the Castle meant the Prague Castle which was and still is the presidential residence, so the slogan meant 'free Havel (and others) from prison and make him the president'.  That was very much about political freedom. They wanted regime change.  Another extremely common slogan was 'End the one-party rule." They wanted democracy and did not want to settle with anything less.
>
