> I grew up in Russia in the 1990s and I would disagree with a couple of minor points in this discussion (overall the lecture is superb). There were plenty of entrepreneurial and business minded young men and women in Russia that could have flourished economically post USSR. The problem was that the country had no idea on how to enforce private property ownership. So racketeering and organised crime sprung up overnight to come and terrorise whatever small business or company was being set up, from market stall to supermarket or restaurant. The organised crime cartels grew and eventually morphed into government, and this paved the way for the oligarcho-capitalist Russia of today which evolved from the criminalised post privatisation Russia of the 90s. About the help of western experts with economic reform - many of them did actually come in 1991, and years after that. Many consultants from American and British investment banks (big names like HSBC) roamed the halls of the ministry of commerce and such at that time advising Russia on how to do privatisation and market integration. Suffice it to say, the result of these "reforms" was a total failure. I don't know who asked them to come, but it's clear (at least now) that the country lacked basic institutions in place before it could or should have been hacked apart and sold on the "free" market to the highest bidder. Neither was anyone particularly interested in nuclear disarmament after 1991. It would have been much easier to force disarmament on Russia at that time with economic measures, than it will be in the coming years (fingers crossed to be wrong on this). So let's praise the Bush/Kohl administration on the Germany deal, but by God let's not forget that the collective west did mess things up an awful lot when it came to its Russia policy with Yeltsin in the 90s.

> When you note that the 2025 Nobel Prizes for Economics are for showing the critical importance of "innovation" and "creative destruction" for economic growth, you also note that the old thinking about economic growth, capital, and labor may be wrong.  Then you note that government institutions are all effective monopolies in their areas, with no competition or failure mechanisms. You can note that the USA, before the recent evolution of the regulatory state, did allow even IBM to effectively kill its own bureaucracy as Apple, Microsoft, etc,  outcompeted IBM.
> 
> This evolution of monopoly institutions into frozen, incompetent organizations seems to explain why socialism/communism can have the best-sounding philosophy and belief system while consistently resulting in zero economic growth and little real innovation.   The USSR had its own IBM equivalent that copied IBM and probably borrowed a bit of IP, like the identical B-29 copy they made.    However, innovation put vacuum tube computers out of the market, and IBM had to adapt or die. By 1980, laptop computers became possible, while the IBM bureaucracy became as slow as any government monopoly, taking 7 years to design a new machine.  IBM owned the universe of my youth, but couldn't adapt to a bunch of bright kids in their parents' garages.   Note: AT&T Bell Labs invented the transistor, but the government monopoly phone systems were the last electronic system to switch to transistors from mechanical systems. 
> 
> Time and innovation played a huge factor in killing the planned economy of the USSR, and the economy killed the political government.   With China now producing massive numbers of high-quality STEM graduates and allowing them freedom to create and innovate in economic areas, our new "industrial planning" regulatory state, where it takes years to decades to get permission to implement any innovation, may fall to the state that allows innovation outside the USA.   China is poised to win, but its internal history of allowing innovation is marginal.

> The point about the various contributions of US administrations leading up to the fall of the Soviet Union is very interesting and seems to have a lot of truth.
> 
> Our system where the pendulum of political opinion seems to swing wildly every 2, 4, 8 years is jarring internally and feels inefficient but it also serves to keep our opponents off balance.  In this sense one might consider this a real advantage in that the US can triangulate onto the right course over time (even if we tend to overdo the reaction to unpopular policy initially).
> 
> Also, the rhetoric of Carter and Reagan seemingly couldn’t be any more different but the underlying power of the government (the bureaucracy and the military - the tribal knowledge) is not so changeable and tends to create stability between administrations.  The ideas and views of a president are what gets attention but, behind the scenes, these are tempered and moderated by the system the president is attempting to control
> 
> These effects can be seen today as well if you look for them.  I think it is something the most pessimistic political observers should keep in mind - a seemingly crazy and bad president will lead to something else and, amongst bad actions and mistakes, can very well contribute something unique and valuable that will (maybe unintentionally) prove useful to the next president

> I can give a little insight of why the Soviets were still spending so much on Nuclear Weapons. In missiles in general, only so many get through. The "enough nukes to destroy the earth multiple times over" number doesn't account for missiles that are intercepted, because those missiles would still spread fallout and contribute to destruction long term. However, Nuclear deterrence is about second strike capacity. You not only need enough nukes to wreck your opponent, you need enough to survive their first strike, and to wreck them through their defenses. The Soviets were paranoid about the West, and they were going to continuously build up their stockpile under the assumption that the US first strike and defenses were getting better all the time.

> As a citizen of the Czech Republic, some moments are almost comical. For example, the astonishment of Soviet politicians that Eastern Europe behaved so… ungratefully.
> 
> Well then… the Czech Republic (or rather Czechoslovakia). We were living quite well, we started building socialism with a human face… and suddenly we hear a knock on the door.
> “Who’s there?” we ask.
> “It’s me, the Soviet Army. We heard you have a problem with capitalism, so I came to help you with that.”
> “That must be a mistake,” we reply.
> “That’s exactly what a capitalist would say! Comrades, we’ve found him—beat that capitalist to death before he infects anyone!”
> “What?” I barely manage to say. The front door flies open, the back door too, a few windows shatter. And tanks and soldiers start flooding into my apartment. Tens of thousands of soldiers. Some even start rappelling down the chimney.
> (Prague — 1968)
> 
> Or should I mention the little “prank” they played on Poland? How they made a deal with Hitler… attacked. Then they rounded up all the captured teachers, doctors, priests, officers—basically everyone—and took them for a walk in the forest. And then they said: “You see that huge pit over there?”
> With a satisfied sigh: “Well, it’s going to be full today.”
> 
> At that time, the Nazis had the opportunity to learn genocide from the already highly experienced USSR. In the Katyn Forest, up to 25,000 Polish prisoners from Poland’s elite were murdered.
> 
> Poland never liked the USSR—there just wasn’t an opportunity for that sentiment to fully manifest.
> 
> As for Ukraine… genocide… Hungary… the massacre during the revolution…
> 
> You know, it’s hard to find anyone in Eastern Europe who didn’t want to see the USSR in ruins.

> @DavidTeng-k7f  You can’t really compare the Austrian empire to the Soviet one. For example, the Czech lands within Austria were like Provence under France, actually in many ways in a better position - richer, with increasingly more independent organisation and with representation in the parliament. You wouldn’t say that “Provence was always controlled by someone: Rome, Paris…”. It’s the same for central Europe: just because Austria-Hungary was called an empire, it doesn’t mean it acted towards its constituents like the other empires. In fact, many of the central European states had their proud and long autonomous tradition and independent statehood. And the Czech lands within the Austrian empire were actually the richest part, except Vienna and Lower Austria, and they had most of the developed industry, highest literacy and flourishing civil society (from the second part of the 19th century). Whereas under Soviet control and communism, the Czech lands plunged from a wealthy and highly developed country to a backwater. We Czechs are very happy the Soviets are gone, and being voluntarily in the EU and NATO is a great benefit for us and we actively worked very hard to get into these voluntary organisations.

I also have issues with the EU, which has a comparable economy to the US, doing very little to deal with the nearby war, and expecting the US to bail them out, while at the same time setting fines on our most innovative companies. We spent our treasure defending them against the Soviet threat, and they invested theirs in their social welfare state under the umbrella of US protection. It's time for them to take on a significant part of the burden so the US can get its house in order. But we should do the flat tax, that part is correct.

> On the soviet work culture in the 1980s: 
> My grandmother said that in the early 1980s many would skip work to go shopping, catch up with friends etc. because there was 0 incentive to work (getting fired is almost impossible, paycheck is stable, promotion tied to years of experience and connections). It was heavily impacting the productivity. So, the government decided to crack down on it by sending police and kgb in civillian clothes to the malls, parks, restaurants. Those caught skipping work would get a fine or bribe the official into letting them go. 
> 
> My father in law, started working at a factory in the 1990, at the age of 16. Often he would simply dip his hands into machine oil at the beginning of his shift (so that it looks like he was doing something) and then hangout with his friends who also worked at this factory for the rest of the day. Yet as his job was considered dangerous (heavy machinery with questionable reliability) he was making a salary of an average engineer.
> 
> My father grew up in a small mining town. There was no street lighting, but in the evening everyone walked with a flashlight. The same type. It couldn't be bought anywhere (legally), but was standard issue for the miners. Because miners got it for free and could always report it as lost in the mine and get a new one, they would sell them very cheaply (for a pack of cigarettes or couple of bottles of vodka).

> @ 16:15 Toynbee's "Civilzations die from suicide, not murder" matches what I have long thought, that the Soviet Union died from socialism.  Socialism does not work.  Reagan's military buildup, US submarines, and all the other shocks hurried up the suicide, but did not murder the Soviet Union.
> 
> Dwarkesh's first interview question is why the Soviet Union lasted so long, and my answer is the same as has propped up every unpopular regime since time immemorial, whether dictatorships or democracies: regimes use outside threats, real or not, to distract the public from domestic troubles.  Stalin and Khrushchev were good at provoking Westerners into taking their bait and overreacting.  Bush Jr used Iraq and Osama bin Laden.  Obama used race.  Trump used (and uses) trade.  Biden used wokism.
> 
> During the interview, Sarah discusses Russia needing a huge army to defend its borders while Britain only needed a small navy.  I have a book somewhere on this, maritime nations vs territorial nations.  Nations with land borders need permanent hierarchical armies, where top-down coordination is vital.  Maritime navies, on the other hand, during the age of sail, might not return for years, and this bred independent thinking, along with making armies smaller and less important.  Russia is the quintessential territorial nation with almost no border security.  Democracy may eventually come of age in Russia, but only after it has had stable land borders for a long long time, and Putin is doing his damnedest to delay that day of stability.

Only in the Brest Fortress, which housed a terrifying NKVD prison, they didn’t manage to liquidate all detainees—some escaped. > It is notable that the broad Soviet partisan movement was organized only in Belarus and partially in ethnically Belarusian lands that were part of the Moscow Empire (Smolensk region, Bryansk region). In the occupied Moscow Empire, there was no partisan movement. Why? Because the plan to exterminate the Belarusian nation continued. Moscow, using NKVD organs, dragged masses of civilian Belarusians into the war against the Germans, thereby exposing Belarusians to German retaliation. A necessary struggle was born of a treacherous scheme and carried out by vile methods. (Stalin wanted to reap double benefit.) > As a result of this joint Bolshevik–fascist “work,” more than 9,000 villages were burned in Belarus. > In the summer of 1944, when the Red Army occupied Belarus, the Muscovites conducted a military mobilization on Belarusian territory. Tens of thousands of young Belarusian men, almost without training, were thrown onto the front lines. > To Sarah's point about conditions in the USSR, as one who came of age during the Cold War I was made aware of the "Music School Effect" so heavily deployed by the Soviets and their proxies. They identified extraordinarily talented people from an early age, primarily in the arts and athletics, and lavished scarce resources on developing them. The Kremlin and other Eastern Bloc governments would then use them as symbolic of the superiority of their societies vis-à-vis the decadent west. We all saw in the Olympics the prowess of the Soviet hockey team, East German swimmers, or Romanian gymnasts, but we weren't fooled into thinking these gifted people represented the average person in their countries. The vanguard of communist artistic and athletic excellence was merely a thin veneer concealing a thoroughly rotten system.

> Ouch. Patel's role here is easy to overlook but it is important.
> First off, not every lecturer on a specific subject  neccessarily has the skillset to promote themselves on social media. Often the more specialized and academic in nature, the more this is true.  Paine doesnt really strike me as someone who is overly concerned with clout, surface style or media optics outside of professionalism.  She's ALL substance and while I find her deadpan sarcasm charming, and she IS likable, she doesnt strike me as a person who notices or cares too much whether people like her. 
> Finding, vetting and "selling" people is also a skill, and in the world of social media, style method counts. Everything from the thumbnail and title presentation that frames your video, down  to the analytics. Ms Paine has spent a lifetime curating her knowlege in universities and libraries and even on the streets of Moscow, and presenting at the Naval Academy.  I dont think she wants or needs a PT job managing an independent media channel. Its a whole additional workload that would presumably be new to her. And while her focus is broad in terms of areas of society affected, she will be the first to admit her knowlege is of specific cultures and periods and currents, predominantly Russian and Japanese history and culture,  and their geopolitical relations with US, China and ec other, mostly from the interwar period through the end of the Cold War, as well as WW2 European theater as well. Patels channel includes other references that go beyond Ms. Paine's specific areas of expertise. 
>    Also Patel asks open ended questions or questions  that, while they may seem uneccessary or sometimes backwards to us, they actually prod or nudge  Paine to explore and speak to the absolute limits of her expertise. Like any professor, she has her "greatest hits" that she reiterates and riffs on, sorta like a leitmotif in music. He asks her unexpected questions and Ive noticed this often engages her to explain things from a different angle than she did before. And while ppl sometimes accuse some of his questions of being odd or backwards, remember, he is trying to ask challenging questions.
>         Finally, as amazing as Ms. Paine is, she is of an older generation than many of, probably most of, Patels listeners. Im probably on the older end of audience and she is a generation older than I.  Sure those of us over 40 into WW2 history wouldve probably eventually stumbled across her if she was on her own channel. 
>  But Patel serves as an important cultural bridge to younger Millenials and Gen Z.  He reached, attracted and cultivated an audience, and it turns out for alot of us, she is our favorite among his channel "topics", and it seems as she becomes a "regular", they are growing the channels audience together now. 
>    While I could listen to her lecture all night, Id also be very interested in Patel identifying other "hidden gems" of lecturers, academics,  policy wonks, geopolitical historians, sociologists, anthropologists, and political scientists and interviewing them or having them do a short lecture to start.
